speechtext: METHADONE AND AMPHETAMINES-STATEMENT ON ACTION TO CONTROL ABUSE	.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister oi National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government, as many members are aware, is deeply concerned about the non-medical use of drugs and the effects of such use on the individual and on our society. As part of our program to combat this hazard through a balanced comprehensive strategy, I wish to announce important action in relation to two different types of drugs, the abuse of which has been a public health problem of major proportions in this country. I refer to action against the abuse of methadone and the amphetamines.
Methadone is an opiate-type synthetic drug which has become widely used in the treatment of heroin addiction. During the last year, staff of my department have received many reports of misuse and abuse of methadone. As a result of concern over misuse of this drug, the former Food and Drug Directorate of my department and the Canadian Medical Association established a joint committee in 1970 to investigate the proper place of methadone in the care of narcotic addicts. Concern about the abuse of methadone also was raised by the Le Dain Commission in its final report on treatment, which was submitted to the government a few weeks ago.
As a result of the recommendations of the joint FDD-CMA committee and of the Le Dain Commission, I have decided to restrict the availability of methadone in the following way: Physicians will be permitted to prescribe methadone only after they are authorized to do so by the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Those so authorized will be considered to be qualified by reason of expertise and the availability of necessary facilities and ancillary services to utilize methadone effectively in the treatment of heroin abuse.
In line with the recommendations of the Le Dain Commission, authorized physicians will be required to be associated with a specialized clinic. Requests for authorization will be considered by an expert advisory committee to be appointed by me in co-operation with the medical profession. I expect that necessary regulatory changes can be made and the methadone control program instituted within a few weeks time. The program should be fully operational by June 1 of this year. In the meantime I call upon the physicians of Canada to utilize restraint in the use of methadone.
Although smaller amounts of amphetamine are now being prescribed in Canada than a few years ago, considerable evidence has come to the attention of my department indicating the over-prescribing of these drugs by some medical practitioners. Considerable evidence also exists that the related drugs, phenmetrazine and phen-dimetrazine, are misused in a manner similar to that of amphetamines.
Medical authorities are agreed that the legitimate medical uses of amphetamines are extremely limited. They have at best only a minor role in rational drug therapy, primarily for the treatment of two relatively rare and obscure disorders, narcolepsy and hyperkinesis in children.
As a result of my grave concern about the serious public health implications of amphetamine abuse, I have decided that the use of amphetamines and the related drugs, phenmetrazine and phendimetrazine, will be limited to treatment of only those disorders for which they are indicated on medical grounds. Use of these drugs for treatment of obesity as so-called "diet pills" will no longer be permitted. Any physician wishing to prescribe amphetamines, phenmetrazine and phendimetrazine will be authorized by the Minister of National Health and Welfare to do so provided he wishes to use the drugs for treatment of bona fide narcoleptics and hyperkinetic children. In co-operation with the Canadian Medical Association and L'Asso-ciation des Medecins de Langue Fran^aise du Canada, a list of consulting physicians will be drawn up to aid in verification of the diagnosis of these relatively rare disorders.
I am extremely pleased with the co-operation being offered to us by the medical associations of Canada in helping solve this important problem.
I am fully aware, as are other hon. members, that this action to control misuse of legally prescribed amphetamines does not directly affect use of these drugs by so-called "speed freaks" who obtain their drugs from illicit sources. Nevertheless, this action does indicate the serious light in which the government views amphetamine abuse and should have marked effects on an important aspect of abuse of these drugs, that by adults who obtain their drugs on prescription.
It will take a few months to work out the details of the amphetamine control program in co-operation with the medical profession. I expect, however, that the program will be fully operational by September 1 of this year.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, may I make a brief mention of another aspect of our total program to control the misuse and abuse of drugs. In January of this year, we invited parents and others receiving federal social assistance cheques to send for a free information booklet entitled "A Parent's Guide to Drug Abuse". Public response to this
198

Control of Drug Abuse
offer has been most gratifying and, in fact, almost overwhelming. To date, nearly 500,000 requests for the booklet have been received by my department and more especially by the directorate on the non-medical use of drugs. Because of the large volume of requests, it is taking my staff longer than they had first anticipated to provide copies of the booklet to all who have requested it. I ask the public to be patient. Everyone who requests a copy of this useful publication will be sent one. This booklet is but the first in a continuing series of factual presentations on various aspects of drug abuse, aimed at providing the facts on this serious problem to Canadians as part of our over-all drug education program.

Mr. Speaker, we cannot help but welcome the statement by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) that his department is deeply concerned about the non-medical use of drugs and the effects on the individual and society.
One of the disturbing things to be noted is that the drug methadone at one time was the cure-all for heroin addicts; addicts were put on this drug so they could be weaned from heroin which was habit-forming. Today we find that methadone is also habit-forming. We wonder in so many cases whether drugs that are being used today which we feel are safe and not habit-forming will turn up tomorrow on the list of those that are habit-forming. The minister will realize that talwin is a drug which could be bought a short time ago without prescription and now is on the prescription list. It was supposed to be a non-habit forming drug. So the story goes.
I wonder whether on the whole we are providing laboratory and research facilities adequate to test the effect of these drugs on human beings. People I have spoken to in this field say that laboratory and research facilities are totally inadequate to test these drugs to determine whether they are or are not habit-forming. I believe the minister realizes this is the situation. He has stated on a number of occasions that more facilities should be provided. However, they are being provided very slowly. I believe this is a very important point.
In bringing these drugs under control I wonder how the minister intends to look after the situation in the Northwest Territories, the Yukon Territory or in other huge and sparsely settled areas which are served by one doctor or even paramedical personnel. I wonder how the people in these areas will be treated and what provisions have been made for treating them. Are they to be brought out to clinics and treated at the expense of the government? The minister did not make this clear.
I also want to dwell for a moment on the fact that the minister has not said very much about the situation of younger people in respect of the use of drugs. I think this is the key to the whole problem. They are growing up in an age in which drugs are thought to be the answer to almost everything and to all problems. I believe it is paramount today that we educate our younger generation in regard to the fact that any drug can be harmful to the human individual. I think this should be part and parcel of the work the minister should carry on in the field of food and drugs. People should be educated that drugs are not the answer to many social problems.
(Mr. Munro.]
I congratulate the minister on this step and suggest to him that we should go further and provide facilities for people living in outlying territories. We should provide laboratory facilities for the treatment of people when they are referred to a lab by a doctor for testing in order to see what the results are, so that more research may be carried on in this field and so that we will have the answers more quickly and not after we find that people are addicts.

Mr. Speaker, I suppose one could start very easily by classifying this statement as a pretty insignificant response to a rather massive problem which has existed in this country for some years and is increasing in intensity as each month goes by. I rather regret the fact that the minister, after examination of the first report of the Le Dain Commission and the treatment report which came out a short while ago, was not able to do better than this in terms of attempting to cope with the non-medical or abusive use of drugs.
[DOT] (i120)
Part of the approach the minister has taken relates to methadone and the dispensing by prescription of methadone as a substitute drug particularly for heroin addicts. Under the proposal the minister will be limiting the opportunity of physicians to dispense and prescribe methadone to specialized clinics. The first thing wrong with that approach is that we will still be using a chemical that will create or help to create a euphoric or semieuphoric condition in the addict himself. We will not be coping whatever in any way with the internal emotional difficulties of addicts that make them addicts in the first place. This is just a stopgap measure. All that will happen, as the minister knows because there has been abuse in the use of methadone itself, is that we will create, in addition to a group of heroin addicts, a group of methadone addicts either in substitution or in addition thereto.
It has been a conscious policy of the Parole Board in issuing parole to addicts who are in penitentiaries to try to place them on parole away from the big, urban metropolitan centres, away from the street, away from the area where drugs are easily available, and parole them to out of the way or smaller communities. If we are going to follow that practice, and I think the Parole Board is, then the minister by this program is denying those heroin addicts who are paroled to out of the way or smaller communities what benefits may arise from a methadone treatment program. He is confining the prescribing of methadone to physicians who are associated with specialized clinics, and the prospects are that the specialized clinics will be in cities like Toronto, Vancouver and Montreal.

them are now undergoing a methadone treatment program through private physicians. If those physicians are to be denied the opportunity to continue to prescribe methadone except in specialized clinics, many of those on parole who are using methadone as a substitute drug for heroin will get into difficulties.
The minister talks in terms of wanting to confine the prescription of amphetamines and other drugs that fall within that class to certain medical uses. I think that is a good move. We have known for a long time that probably the people who have contributed most in a total sense to the thinking of society that you can cure anything with a pill have been those in the medical profession who have dispensed pills, potions and lotions without full knowledge of their effects. The attempt now to confine this is a good measure. I hope doctors will pay heed to it. I hope also that drug manufacturers will be required to provide more information on the side effects of drugs that are developed and used for such purposes.
It seems to me that the minister's statement does not really cope with the underlying reason why people want to drop out of society, why they want to use drugs, why they want to create a false feeling within themselves, why they want to escape from the realities of the world. This action is simply a small patchwork program in light of the over-all problem. It is necessary to engage in an educational program, to try to explain and to get people to understand what the realities of life are all about, and not just approach the problem by using one drug as a substitute for the other.
I wish that the minister had taken the course in this statement-it is long overdue-of rejecting the proposal in the LeDain Commission report which suggests that we give a semi-legal status to heroin so that as a last resort, whether it be in specialized clinics or elsewhere, a heroin addict who fails to agree with the methadone treatment, program can get heroin itself. That recommendation should have been rejected by the minister as soon as it was made. The absence of any comment in this document on this matter means two things. The moment the LeDain Commission recommendation was made with respect to classifying or giving heroin some sort of semi-legal status, it was applauded by every heroin addict in the country because they foresaw the prospect of being able, in time of short supply of heroin, to proceed to treatment centres and get free fixes to carry them over a period of time until the supply increases.
I know that you are getting apprehensive about the time I am taking, Mr. Speaker, but to me this is an extremely important matter which was left out of the statement and should have been in it. I will only be a moment more, if I may.
The other point is that a number of young people in our society are on the borderline; they are unsure whether they should try heroin, having used other drugs. When the LeDain commission report on treatment came out and gave some sanction in its recommendations to the use of heroin, a number of young people in this nation in the drug scene said: This is fine, heroin is O.K., it has the endorsement of the LeDain commission.
Some addicts in the city of Vancouver whom I know, people in the addict world and people trying to do some-
Control of Drug Abuse
thing about it, know that a number of youngsters applauded that recommendation. They were unable to draw the distinction between the commission report and government policy and began trying heroin themselves because it had some sort of semi-legal sanction. Every day the minister delays in rejecting that concept he is contributing to the growing population of youngsters who are trying heroin. I wish the minister would abandon this insignificant patchwork program and out of his conscience do something worth while for a change instead of announcing such piddling measures.

Mr. Speaker, I would like first of all to thank the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) for the measures announced today to control the abuse of methadone and amphetamines.
We are particularly happy about the valuable and essential co-operation of medical associations. Without their powerful participation, the announcement made today by the minister would only be empty words.
That measure announced today will have the effect of restraining the "official" availability of those particular drugs, but as the minister himself recognized it, that does not affect at all use of those drugs by addicts who get them from illicit sources. There lies the main weakness of governmental action with regard to the control of the distribution and illegal consumption of various drugs in Canada, specially among the young.
Today's statement, Mr. Speaker, should not make us forget what the federal government did in that field.
Indeed, an official OPTAT inquiry revealed the following:
A comparison of results obtained in 1969 and 1971 shows that:
Consumption of barbiturates has tripled and that of hallucinogens other than LSD almost tripled:
Consumption of marijuana and LSD had more than doubled;
It has increased by a third in the case of stimulants and tranquilizers;
It has increased by almost one tenth in the case of alcohol and tobacco;
the proportion of a glue consumers was the same in 1971 as in 1969.
Consequently, government action in that sphere is still pending, and statements in fact merely constitute a control of official prescriptions but in no way-which is more serious-do they affect illegal consumption.
In closing, I quote an excerpt taken from an article published in La Boussole, of Nicolet, on December 11, 1968:
Here is what Dr. Homes had to say during a panel discussion at which the medical profession was recognized as a leader in the fight against toxicomania:
"Although we usually speak of toxicomania as a disease, it is more specifically the symptom of a disease rooted in social and economic conditions that tend to create dissatisfaction, sadness, conflicts and tensions in the very soul and spirit of human beings.
This means that one of the greatest experts in this field states that the source of that insecurity is ascribable to the social insecurity from which young Canadians are suffering at the present time. Neither the family nor other voluntary organizations dealing with drugs can do any-

In this regard, Mr. Speaker, so long as the federal government merely takes steps in co-operation with medical organizations and associations to control consumption and distribution of drugs legally prescribed, so long as it does not take any drastic steps to control unlawful consumption and distribution, so long as it fails to take economic and social measures enabling young Canadians to live in economic and social security, so long as it continues marking time on this issue, the government will be channeling Canadians towards the use of drugs.
That is why we are concerned with the government's attitude, its apathy, its complacency in regard to the findings of the LeDain report. We are anxious to know, at the earliest, the position of the government which is hedging behind the report for the purpose of obtaining the votes of young people, whereas I consider saving these young people and giving them security to be more important than securing their votes.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43 I ask the unanimous consent of the House to propose a motion on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity to the Atlantic provinces. It arises out of the latest increase in rail freight rates, the eighth in the past 29 months, and the imminence of a further 2.5 per cent decrease in subsidies and a corresponding increase in freight rates. Since these increases have worked hardship on industries in the area and are prejudicial to the public interest I would move, seconded by the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester North (Mr. Coates):
That this House urge the government to immediately impose a freeze on rail freight rates until a new Atlantic transportation policy, embodying the proposals of the twelfth report of the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications, is formulated.

speechtext: The House resumed, from Wednesday, February 23, consideration of the motion of Mr. Ross Whicher for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity and privilege to take part in the debate on the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. First, of course, I should like to express my deepest appreciation for the contributions made by the mover and the seconder of the address in reply. I am particularly interested in the fact that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) took the time to give some information regarding the hon. member for Bruce (Mr. Whicher). I note he indicated to the House that this member had sat in the provincial house from 1955, I believe, until 1967 and was then elected to the House of Commons in 1968.
When I listened to the hon. member's speech and then reread it I could readily understand why he was in the opposition in the Ontario Legislature for such a lengthy period of time. There are two particular statements I should like to bring back to haunt the hon. member. First of all, as recorded at page 9 of Hansard, he said:
Without any doubt I can say here this afternoon that the senior citizens of Canada have the benefit of the just society promised by our government.
Mr. Speaker, that is one of the more irresponsible statements I have heard since I have been here. I do not know where the hon. member lives or why he has not received the same type of mail I have received from these poor, frustrated Canadians, frustrated because of the attitude of this government in terms of lack of senior citizen housing, in terms of the high cost of living and in terms of removing the escalation clause in respect of the minimum old age security payment. These people constantly write to me and I am sure to all other hon. members. So far as I am concerned they do not believe they are living in a just society and they are not likely to do so in the very near future unless there is a change of government.
I should like to bring up another matter.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
There is the man of the cloth. I read the editorial about him. I will let my remarks stand. I support the editorial fully. It appears that the hon. member will not be back with us for the glory and edification of the people of Canada after the next election.
Let me quote another statement made by the hon. member for Bruce. As recorded at page 13 of Hansard, he said:
When the chips are down, the people of Canada will appreciate the good life that this government is allowing them to live.
I underline the word "allowing". Is that a responsible statement? I wonder whether in fact this is the fact. Is "Trudeaucracy" allowing the people of Canada to live? Let me set the hon. member straight because if they are living they are living in extremely adverse conditions. It is no wonder the Prime Minister has indicated he will not go to the people on his past record but rather intends to
February 24, 1972

concentrate on future plans. If we look at this matter of allowing people to live and the record of the government in terms of human frustration and alienation, we can readily understand why all of us wait with baited breath his announcement of the next election.
Just let me point out the dismal failure of the government in certain areas, and this must be repeated and repeated again because these are the issues about which people are concerned. This government is possessed of certain highs, such as high taxes, the high number of bankruptcies and lay-offs, the high payment they gave to old age pensioners amounting to 42 cents, and high unemployment. At present 665,000 are unemployed. The Prime Minister has said this is a regrettable side effect of the government's fiscal and monetary policies. What concerns me is the fact that those who are deserving and should be rewarded are not considered. There is the case of Mr. Vallieres. For the life of me I do not know what was the philosophy behind hiring him, particularly when I hear the then Minister of Labour condone such action and tell us that this type of person is more worthy than Lord knows how many unemployed of whom there are about 10 per cent to 12 per cent in the province of Quebec. The minister has condoned this action and I for one do not accept it. This is the kind of climate in which we are living as a result of this government's involvement with the destiny of the people of Canada.
We have also had lows. There is the low in the confidence of Canadians in the government. There is the alienation that exists in the west. We all know about that because we have all travelled out west. There is also the alienation that exists in central Canada as a result of the rigidity of this government, and the alienation that exists in the Atlantic provinces as a result of this government being bankrupt of ideas to solve or reduce regional economic disparities.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Of course there is also a new low in Canada-United States relations. But then I wonder what we can expect when we find that the Prime Minister on an overseas tour registered some concern vis-a-vis our American friends when he stated that he fears a cultural, economic and military take-over by that country. This is the gist of the message. We cannot wonder then at this new low in U.S.-Canadian relations and at the fact that Canadians have to suffer a little pain. We should reiterate and re-emphasize to our American friends that we are their best trading customers. We must tell them that if we have to suffer any pain they in turn will suffer pain also as a result of their economic policies that hamstring us.
I should like to make a few comments with regard to the employment record of this government. The Prime Minister, in his reply to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) the other day, had much to say about gloom and doom. Surely it is the role of the opposition to point out the inadequacies and failures of this government. If in our words there is gloom, perhaps there is need for gloom when there are some 665,000 people out of work. It is not only the individual who is out of work that we have to consider but, as I have stated continually, we have to go
Speech from the Throne
down the ladder and consider the bus driver, the taxicab driver, the corner grocery store owner and the small businessmen whose livelihood depends on the income or lack of it of the 665,000. We get confused and we say that there are only 665,000 people out of work, but this is the nitty-gritty of our economic stability because without these people being able to purchase goods and services the economy founders.
On page 2 of Hansard for February 17, 1972 there is a reference in the Throne Speech to "our success ... in the creation of new jobs". The next day the Prime Minister expanded on this theme and said:
The large number of new jobs being created in Canada should not be overlooked.
If anyone is overlooking anything, it is the Prime Minister; he is the one who is ignoring facts. The Economic Council of Canada has estimated that during the period from 1970 to 1975 the rate of employment growth needed to absorb the labour force growth and to reduce unemployment to about 4 per cent would be about 3.3 per cent per year. In 1970 employment increased by 1.3 per cent, and in 1971 employment increased by 2.5 per cent. Only 299,000 jobs were created in 1970 and 1971 together-a mere 21 per cent of the 1.4 million we need by 1975. Accordingly, there is a gap of 1.1 million jobs to be bridged in the next three years if we are to reduce unemployment to a more acceptable level.
What does this shortfall in job creation mean in human terms? It means that only 64 per cent of all labour force entrants in the past two years have found jobs. It means that only half of all men entering the labour force between the beginning of 1970 and the end of 1971 found jobs. It means that only 46 per cent of all young people entering the labour force in these two years found jobs, which is tragic, to say the very least.
Since the Prime Minister took office at the beginning of May, 1968, employment has risen by 5.5 per cent, the labour force has shot up by 9 per cent and consequently unemployment has almost doubled, rising from 366,000 in May, 1968, to the present figure of 665,000 in January, 1972. This is the record on which the Prime Minister wants to stand. This is the record about which he boasts.
The Prime Minister admonishes Canadians not to overlook:
... the fact that, between 1965 and 1970-the last period for which statistics are available-over one million new jobs were created in Canada.
Perhaps this is the problem with the government's policies on unemployment. The Prime Minister is now aware that Canada's employment and unemployment figures are available right up to January, 1972, and consequently he is acting on the basis of long outdated figures. Canada's job creation, the Prime Minister continues, was much faster than in other countries between 1965 and 1970. Maybe this is true, but few other countries in the world have a labour force growth as rapid as Canada's and few have an unemployment rate as high as Canada's.
The Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development published in May, 1970, their projections for needed employment growth in their member countries between 1970 and 1975. These projections show that Canada was far ahead of all other industrial countries in

February 24, 1972
Speech from the Throne
the need for employment growth during the decade. I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that these projections show that Canada was far ahead of all other industrial countries in the need for employment growth during the decade. Between 1970 and 1975 Canada's needed employment growth was estimated at 15 per cent compared with only 9 per cent for the United States and no more than 5 per cent for any other country. Obviously, then, other countries in the 1970s do not need to aim as high in employment growth as does Canada because their labour forces are not growing as fast. This is the point that I believe the Prime Minister deliberately missed. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister's pleasure at Canada's employment growth rate is rather hollow and meaningless.
Of more relevance is another figure, the ratio of unemployed people to vacancies in various countries. The most recent figures in this regard are for the third quarter of 1971. They show that in the European countries the Prime Minister referred to in his reply to the Leader of the Opposition, being Belgium, France, Sweden, Germany, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom but excluding Italy for which there were no job vacancy figures, there is a vast difference in the competition for available jobs. In these European countries there were only 1.3 unemployed persons competing for each vacant job whereas in Canada at the same time there were 10.6 unemployed persons competing for each vacant job. Quite a difference in this regard.
There is another way to view the Trudeau employment record, and that is by comparing the rate of growth of employment, the rate of growth of the labour force, and employment rates during the Trudeau years with the records of previous Canadian governments. There were several years in the pre-Trudeau era which managed a higher rate of employment growth and a lower unemployment rate even when the labour force was growing faster than today.
I refer you to the year 1966, Mr. Speaker, when we had an annual increase in the labour force of 3.9 per cent and an annual increase in employment of 4.2 per cent and an unemployment rate of 3.6 per cent. So we see that in 1966 Canada's employment growth was faster than anything in the Trudeau years. In spite of the fact that her labour force grew faster than in any year since, the unemployment rate was lower than any annual rate the Trudeau government has been able to show.
Rather than look at all these facts and at Canada's 665,000 unemployed, the Prime Minister prefers to tell the nation that every cloud has its silver lining. Why do the unemployment figures matter, he implies, when Canada's international record in employment growth from 1965 to 1970 is unsurpassed?
More than this, the Prime Minister has recently been repeatedly telling the unemployed that jobs are available but they are too lazy to get them. The great mining centres of Canada such as Sudbury, he says, are crying for workers. The fact that INCO has been planning and carrying out lay-offs for several months has done little to dampen his enthusiasm for this approach to the unemployment problem. The Prime Minister and his advisers, before he visits and insults the unemployed in this manner, at least

in Ontario, should read the recently released report of the Ontario task force on employment opportunities for welfare recipients, especially page 67 where it is stated:
There is comparatively large-scale unemployment now affecting all areas of the province, if not to the same extent elsewhere, to the extent that no area has a shortage of labour.
Sincerely, Mr. Speaker, Canadians have heard enough of the Trudeau government's misleading figures and its excuses.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Canadians need and want a comprehensive set of policies to deal with the problem, not a re-run of the old rhetoric that tries to sweep the problem under the rug and away from the government's hands. "Out of sight, out of mind" seems to be the Trudeau government philosophy toward unemployment.
I understand that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) wants to speak immediately after me. Perhaps he will give some indication of the industrial policy that the government intends to implement in order that we can have economic growth and full employment. I should like to hear what the Minister of Finance has to say about full employment. As I said, "out of sight, out of mind" seems to be the Trudeau government philosophy toward unemployment and every statement in the throne speech is dedicated to that end.
The present Canadian ills of high unemployment and rising prices are the products of the anaemic and petty economic policies of the Trudeau government. The issue now is whether those policies are changing. I do not believe they are.
I know that the Minister of Finance is waiting most anxiously to state the direction in which this great country should be pointed under the present regime and we are waiting with bated breath for his speech. I know that the former Minister of Justice in his new position as Minister of Finance will display the same compassion and the same humanitarian feeling toward the Canadian people as he has in the past.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
This is what we are talking about- people. I know the Minister of Finance is concerned and what he has to say to us this afternoon will be on the record for the edification of all of us. I hope the recent change in the finance portfolio is of some significance.
I should like to tell the minister of a meeting I attended in the city of Hamilton not too long ago. I hope other members will have the same sort of meeting because I found it most gratifying, informative and interesting. The labour community was invited but unfortunately did not see fit to attend. If we want to move toward some co-operation, negotiation and understanding between labour, business, government and management, I am at a loss to understand why labour did not attend.
The businessmen were concerned because they were being bombarded by an excessive amount of legislation that, as they said, left them no time to run their businesses. They placed great emphasis on the tax bill which was recently implemented by closure; they also placed great emphasis on the competition bill and its dire effects,
February 24, 1972

with particular reference to the tribunal. They referred to the labour bill with its features regarding technological change and referred to high management being unionized. They were concerned about the poor draftmanship in these bills. In at least one instance, the tax bill recently forced upon us, I know this is to be true. We know that the bill is not in a perfect state and that amendments have been made to amendments to amendments and that there will be further amendments. But the government has the gall to say that they have removed any uncertainty from the business sector and from the private sector, meaning the individual. How can there be any confidence, how can they say that there is no uncertainty when there are still amendments pending?
Another point they brought up, Mr. Speaker, is the fact that this government does not listen to the points brought out in the briefs submitted. They hear the phrase "participatory democracy" and are invited to send their briefs, but they indicated to me that they believe this means nothing because the briefs are thrown in the wastepaper basket. I have already said that all the brains in this country are not in the House of Commons.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Not on the other side, anyway.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: There are brains outside this place; as a matter of fact, there are more outside than inside. The government would be well advised to pay more attention, and particularly the hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. McBride). I told the House what is going to happen to him. Another matter they were concerned about was the philosophy of this government. They do not know what that philosophy is.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: They don't have one.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I cannot tell you. I want you to tell the Canadian people. What is your philosophy? Where are you going?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Where are you going? You have the whole country upset and frustrated about what Canada is going to be like in the next six years.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: They are going out in the cold; that is where they are going.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to let you know that Hamilton is concerned about the economic climate. As an industrial city it is extremely concerned, obviously, about the type of legislation that is introduced, the philosophy behind it and whether it provides any incentives. Mr. Speaker, as a member of this government since it took office in 1968, and indeed of the previous government under Mr. Pearson, I have had close contact for some years with the economic and financial issues that confront us. While I am familiar with the problems, I recognize that I have a lot of homework to do on the matters that are the particular responsibility of the Minister of Finance.
I also recognize that I have a lot of hard thinking to do on the best means of dealing with the central economic and financial problems facing the country. I want to assure the House that about such questions my mind is receptive to the best counsel I can get from any quarter. I start from the premise that no one, nowhere, has a monopoly on wisdom. I begin with a good many convictions but with an open mind.
In my judgment, the first responsibility of this portfolio concerns the management of the Canadian economy as a whole. As I see it, the prime objective of economic management is to obtain the greatest increase in jobs, in production and in the real income of Canadians that it is possible to achieve on a continuing basis. Setting the objective of economic policy is easy; attaining that objective is immensely complex and difficult, judging not only from our own experience in this country but from the experience of all nations.
It is not a problem that will yield to simplistic solutions, solutions that ignore the realities of the world in which we
Speech from the Throne
live. In pursuit of this objective it is important to recognize that the Canadian economy does not operate in isolation nor in accordance with the dictates of Ottawa. On the contrary, the national economy is exposed to many forces both at home and abroad which restrict the federal government's ability to control the direction of that economy with infinite precision.
Ours is essentially a free enterprise economy, not one whose every movement is determined by the state. Certainly, the federal government will play the central role in guiding its course, but every day millions of Canadian consumers-workers, farmers, fishermen, businessmen, investors-make individual decisions in the marketplace which over time have a massive impact on the state of our whole economy.

Provinces and municipalities also have great influence. How much tax they levy, how much they spend, how much and where they borrow-all those decisions have a bearing on the workings of the economic system. Twenty years ago, those two levels of government spent only about 36 per cent of every Canadian tax dollar. Today the ratio is about 60 per cent. Now that provinces and municipalities spend .half as much again as the federal government they are in a position where their impact on Canadian economic activity is substantial to say the least.
On the other hand, our economy is far from isolated from the rest of the world. We are probably more than any other nation influenced by the international economic environment. We are a trading nation by necessity, and 25 cents out of every dollar we make comes from abroad. In 1969, export of Canadian products yielded the equivalent of $653 for every man, woman, and child in Canada. Although Japan is considered as one of the world's great trading nations, its export revenues for the same year were only $187 per capita. Moreover, we are deeply affected not only by trade variations but also by the decisions of other capital cities and financial centres of the world. The actions of governments in Washington, Tokyo, London, Paris and Bonn, the decisions made by businessmen and financiers in New York, Chicago, Hambourg, Rotterdam and Zurich can all have a bearing on our prosperity here in Canada.
It must be recognized that there is a fourth and universal constraint on the ability of all governments to ensure that the economy achieves the desired course at all times. That constraint is the limit of knowledge. Medical men have not yet learned all there is to know about medicine, nor economists about economics, even though great strides have been made in both fields over the past several decades.

I fully recognize that statistics are no substitute for jobs. But if we are to deal in a realistic way with the manpower problems confronting us, I think it is essential to recognize how extraordinary they are in nature. They stem primarily from the fact that for a number of years Canada's labour force has been growing far more quickly than that of any other industrialized nation in the world. The Economic Council of Canada has estimated that between 1965 and 1980 the total increase in Canada's labour force in absolute terms will exceed that of Britain, West Germany and Italy combined by some 20 per cent, even though the present population of those countries is around eight times that of Canada. The problem in Canada is compounded by the severe impact of winter on employment in many fields, by the vastness of our nation and by the limited economic opportunities in some regions of the country. The quickening pace of economic growth is now absorbing more and more of our unused human and material resources. As the expansion continues, however, we will begin to face a new threat to our prosperity, that of renewed rises in costs and prices.
During 1970 and 1971 Canada's price performance surpassed that of every other industrialized nation. But in
Speech from the Throne
recent months there has been some acceleration in the rate of Canadian price increases. Although this is partly attributable to special factors relating to food, there has also been a sufficient increase in other sectors to provide a warning signal. This leads me to what in my judgment is the fundamental problem of economic management. This is the problem of maintaining maximum growth of employment and production in the economy, while at the same time preventing the development of inflationary pressures which eventually could undermine the very foundations of the economy if allowed to go unchecked. To keep the problem in perspective, it should be remembered that substantial progress has already been made during the postwar period in reducing the violent swings from boom to bust that used to be experienced in western economies.
But we still have some way to go in achieving strong, but stable economic growth on a sustained basis. In some respects, the job of maintaining strong but stable economic growth has become tougher to deal with than ever before. Certainly, this has been the experience of many nations in recent years and the conclusion of two major international bodies, the International Monetary Fund and the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. The problem is that once inflation has been set in motion by excessive demands on a country's real capacity to produce goods and services, it tends to continue to accelerate long after these demands have been brought back into closer balance with productive capacity. Costs continue to chase prices and prices to chase costs around and around in an everrising spiral. This strong, pervasive and stubbornly persistent kind of cost-push inflation represents a new element, a new kind of force working on our economy. Cost-push inflation has frequently occurred to some extent in the past, but more recently it has taken on a far more virulent form. Just as no one fully understands the reasons for this development, neither is there any clear consensus about how best to bring it under control without causing long-term damage to the economy as a whole.
Resolving the problem of restoring and maintaining full employment while avoiding the risks of inflation is a matter of fundamental concern. I have requested officials of my department to take a new look at the anatomy of unemployment and inflation as a matter of priority to see whether we can suggest what needs to be done to create productive jobs for those who want to work without causing an excessive erosion in the value of the income and savings of ordinary Canadians.

There are other long-term problems which we must face. Some are urgent for the only reason that in the world we live in, time and space are increasingly compressed. Changes are quickly occurring everywhere. Tomorrow can at any time become today. Those considerations are as applicable to our economy as to other aspects of our community. They are evident in the scientific and technological fields. They are evident in the outstanding role which the multinational corporations are called to play and the division of various countries throughout the world into trade blocs.
If we refuse to fall back in that race, we must meet the challenge raised by changes around us. It has sometimes

Speech from the Throne
been suggested that some of the steps which we proposed in this regard have created a climate of uncertaincy prejudicial to business matters and the economy. As I have said before, I understand that need for stability. It is in the nature of man and institutions to try to resist change, to cling to the familiar, the tested, the conventional wisdom applicable to yesterday's problems. But I also know that if we stick to the status quo, if we refuse to face the challenges of relentless changes in our midst, there is but one certainty-eventual economic stagnation. I feel there should be more understanding in our country with regard to the need for adopting to progress and evolution. That does not mean, however, that no room should be left for discussion between reasonable men on how to meet the imperatives of those changes. I therefore expect in this regard, constructive suggestions from every quarter.
Among other things, we should consider how our industrial policy should evolve in this world of progress, to achieve a better distribution and a more efficient exploitation of our resources, human as well as material. We should find the means to encourage the development of technology, production and employment in those sectors that offer the best possibilities for increasing our competition with other countries. We must continue to press toward the reorganization of several industries, for greater specialization and production, so that Canadian products might be more competitive on both domestic and international markets.

The formation of commercial policy, which is an integral part of our over-all economic policies is, in conjunction with the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) a special responsibility of the Minister of Finance. I intend to devote careful attention to our commercial policy. The division of the world into large trading blocs, to which I referred a few moments ago, presents particular dangers to Canada as a major trading nation and one of the few industrialized countries without free access to a market of 100 million people or more. The unwinding of the international crisis that posed such a serious threat to the maintenance of the post-war trade and payments system for several months during the latter half of 1971 has been a matter of considerable relief and satisfaction. We in this country must now use what influence we can bring to bear to press for a resumption of the postwar movement toward greater liberalization of international trade. The dangerous alternative would be a move backward toward greater protectionism. This alternative would present a serious threat to our economy and certainly thwart our efforts to bring about greater diversification of our trade.
The House is well aware that there still remain outstanding issues involving bilateral trade relationships between Canada and the United States. As my colleague, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce has made clear, we remain hopeful that a number of these issues between us can be resolved to the mutual benefit of both countries. May I add that I much appreciate the efforts made to explain Canada's position and its point of view by those members of this House and of the other place who met recently with their counterparts from Washington on the Canada-U.S. interparliamentary group.

We are also giving very careful consideration to the implications for Canada of the United States so-called DISC legislation. This seems to me to be a rather thinly disguised export subsidy. As an exporting country we must be concerned about the world's greatest industrial nation resorting to such a practice. We have already received a number of helpful representations from Canadian businessmen. My senior officials are now making a detailed examination, with the assistance of knowledgeable people in the business community, of the likely impact of DISC on our exports to third markets, on production in Canada for the Canadian market, and on the prospects for potential plant expansion.
I do not wish to forecast at this stage what the results of this detailed investigation are likely to be, nor what policy we will be proposing.
One of my important responsibilities relates to the custody of our newly reformed tax system. Without going into all the wide variety of social measures which we will have brought forward during this Parliament, I might point out that this new system by itself rebuts the allegation in the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) that this government has deepened the gap between the affluent and those in need. Tax reform has resulted in taxes being reduced or eliminated for 5,700,000 Canadians.
One million Canadians have been removed from the income tax rolls completely. A special tax relief of a substantial nature was provided for hundreds of thousands of elderly Canadians. At the same time, the tax reform provided that those who were affluent would bear a fairer share of the load. The allegations made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) simply collapse under the weight of the facts.
Any piece of legislation that is so mammoth and so complex is bound to raise problems. This was fully recognized by my predecessor who gave a commitment to examine a variety of areas in which problems might arise. I am quite prepared to live up to that commitment and to consider adjustments to the law, provided that those adjustments do not sacrifice the underlying principles of reform, where it can be shown that its application had unforeseen and unreasonable consequences. I have asked the new minister of state, whom the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) kindly assigned to help me and who performed so ably in helping to pilot the tax reform legislation through the House, to take on the initial task of examining the problems that may exist and the steps that might be considered to correct them.

In our approach to the various problems we face, it will be essential to establish improved communication and better understanding between the government and other sectors of the economy in order to develop the basis of better co-operation. We are all in the same boat and I believe we are rowing on the whole in the same direction. What we should focus on is a greater agreement on the means of reaching our goal.
First and foremost there should be co-ordination and closer links between federal and provincial governments
February 24, 1972

on the policies and programs likely to affect the economy. My first task on taking up my present assignment was to chair the annual economic and fiscal conference of provincial ministers of finance and treasurers.
In the discharge of the responsibilities involved in my previous portfolio, I attended, with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) several lengthy conferences concerning the revision of the Canadian constitution.

speechtext:
I want to thank the House for its courtesy.

But the discussions held in Jasper served to convince me, once again, that arrangements, with regard to taxes, expenditures and other financial questions between the two levels of government are the keystone of our Confederation. Such relations are vital for a proper division of powers and responsibilities between Ottawa and the provinces. I shall give more information on this subject in the next few days, when I introduce a bill providing for the extension and improvement of such financial agreements between the two levels of government.
Apart from working in closer co-operation with the provinces, I would also like to take part in the development of closer relations between the federal government and other sectors, such as business and labour. The government's primary objective is to promote the national interest by the best and most effective means available.
So, I very strongly hope to benefit from representations and advice from the business community, labour unions, farmers' and consumers' groups and others on the policies and programs that are needed in order to best serve national interest. I realize, of course, that one problem remains: that of reconciling opposite interests of different groups and their often conflicting views on the best way of contributing to national interest. However, as better communications link us, it should be possible to develop a wider base of agreement on what we should do to serve public interest together.

Almost every decision faced by the government involves finding a reasonable balance between competing rights and claims that will best serve the interests of the nation as a whole. As Minister of Justice, I found that most of the decisions I had to take involved a judgment weighing individual liberty on the one hand and the welfare and safety of the community on the other. These judgments were not easy and, although they were made with the best of intentions, I am sure they were not always right.
In my new portfolio, I expect that I will also have to seek a balance between other claims that may at times
Speech from the Throne
conflict, for example, between incentive and economic growth on the one hand and equity and redistribution of national wealth on the other. I hope that the policies for which I am responsible will help to ensure the maintenance of a fair and improving standard of living for every Canadian without impeding the economic growth that is a prerequisite for raising the quality of life in the nation as a whole.
I accepted this portfolio because I believe that the major issues facing Canadians for a number of years to come will be economic, that in the final analysis it will be the bread and butter issues that count. That is not to say I believe that the life style issues with which I have had to deal in the House and in the country in the last three and a half years have now become irrelevant-by no means. The quality of our lives is pertinent and relevant to any civilized people. But quality cannot be enjoyed unless there is an underpinning of economic sufficiency.
In that context I want to conclude by pointing out that the Canadian economy is not, as the opposition would have it, weak and growing weaker. Quite the contrary, it is strong and growing stronger. I have said that in taking hold of my new responsibilities, I see our first priority to be to provide good jobs for Canadians who are seeking work. This we will do and we shall try our best to do it without inducing an erosion in the purchasing power of the incomes and savings of the average working man and his family. I count on the support of this House in moving toward that goal.

speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I wish I could congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) on the statement he made today to the effect that our economy is growing stronger and that his first priority is to create jobs for Canadians. Unfortunately, I cannot do that because his predecessor made this same statement in the House at least a dozen times, that our economy was growing stronger and would create jobs. The time now is for action, Mr. Speaker. What we need is action and not empty rhetoric. If the minister does come forth with specific legislation for the creation of jobs, I am sure all of us on this side of the House will join in applauding him.
This is the fourth Speech from the Throne during the term of this Prime Minister and most of us expect it to be the last before a general election is called some time in 1972. This gives us an opportunity to assess the government's activities over the last three years, as well as the opportunity to offer some alternatives. These have been disappointing years to say the least, wasted years-perhaps even dangerous years to the future of our country when you look at the long term values. In 1968, because of his style and acting ability, the Prime Minister personified the change that Canadians wanted. They wanted a new direction after centennial year, a break with the past, an innovator. The Prime Minister realized this and capitalized on the hunger for change, but he has completely failed to satisfy this appetite in the people.
I remember very well my maiden speech in this House when I spoke about the young people of this country and what I thought they wanted, what they expected of this place, of parliamentarians and of the government. I should like to read one short paragraph from that speech which I thought was a challenge to the government and to Members of Parliament. At that time I said:
For young people democracy is on trial right here and now. We have heard a lot about alienation, about frustration, student unrest, riots, hippies and similar groups within the youth com-

munity. All of these phenomena are important to this House for one reason. That reason is that the verdict on the democratic system by many of these young people has already been made and that verdict is guilty-guilty of irrelevance, guilty of lack of purpose, guilty of lack of meaning for their lives but, most important of all, the political system has been found guilty for its failure to produce results here and now.
That was one of the challenges that faced the government when it took office in 1968. The political process had to prove itself, not just to the young people of the country but to many others. As Members of Parliament we had to prove ourselves to the people. Politicians could no longer get away with some of the half-truths and the old rhetoric of days gone by. I feel quite sincerely that the government has failed to meet this challenge; they have failed rather miserably.
We find that the young people in the country are still cynical and that this cynicism has spread to other groups, the western farmer, the worker, the unemployed, the poor, the Indian and Metis. This feeling of despair that Ottawa does not really care about them is real, and it is by no means an accident. I think that the Prime Minister must bear responsibility for it because it was he who tantalized the imagination of many Canadians with new approaches and style. He brought many people to a high level of expectation in 1968 and then let them drop.
The campaign of 1968 caught the mood and the tune of centennial year, the mood of optimism, of innovation, of the future. Sensing this, the Prime Minister picked up the mood and promised action in three broad areas; first, national unity; second, the just society and, third, participatory democracy. I suggest that these have all been monumental failures, disasters, and each of these themes is returning to haunt Liberal Members of Parliament. I should like to look at each of these themes later in my speech, Mr. Speaker.
The Speech from the Throne leaves me cold, and I am sure it leaves most of the Canadian people out in the cold. It is similar to every Throne Speech delivered since this Prime Minister came to power. It is full of flowery rhetoric and self-praise, as well as references to our great and rosy future. I do not think I am being unkind when I say that I get the image of the Prime Minister as the selfappointed philosopher king who feels he has a divine right to govern. I think I even see some of that in the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) when he said today, "We will look after you; don't worry about it, we are going to create jobs*' and so on.
Every so often this philosopher king descends from his throne, and condescends to lecture the members of this House in a professorial manner, telling us not to worry, that things will be better, that life in Canada is second to none-perhaps second only to Heaven itself. The Throne Speech was full of this and it is the kind of rhetoric that has been given the Canadian people for the past three years. That attitude of divine right is being transmitted to some cabinet ministers. A short while ago in Vancouver when speaking about the economy the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) sais that there was nothing wrong with the economy, that it was in good shape and it was time Canadians woke up to this fact. I suggest that exactly the reverse it true. It is time the government woke up to the fact that the economy is not in good shape. I
February 24, 1972

think the people know that and will not tolerate this kind of approach much longer.
In these days of mass communications, new technology and modern education, people are aware of the conditions that exist. They are aware of what can and should be done. The voter in Canada is well informed and knows that we can do better. For example, he knows that in this country there is a great deal of wealth, technology and education, and that if we wanted to change the country socially and economically we could do so in a massive way and could do it immediately.
Mr. Speaker, we all know that some changes have been made. Any government will make a few changes. We have had recognition of China, a few winter works programs and the establishment of DREE, which was a failure but at least it was established. We have had a few patches here and there on the economy in an effort to fix up the system. That is not good enough.
What I want, what our party wants and what I am sure in increasingly large numbers the Canadian people want, is an overhaul of the entire system; a new system of government, a new approach. Patches are not good enough for most people in Canada. The unemployed want jobs, not just fancy rhetoric or the Minister of Finance talking about jobs that will be created some time in the future. They want jobs now. The farmer wants a farm that is economic and viable; the poor want opportunities and they are not getting them; the Indian and Metis people are tired of rhetoric and want action; Quebec, the Prairies and the Maritimes want to be equal partners within Confederation. Perhaps most important of all, more and more Canadians want our country to be independent, economically and socially, from the multinational corporations. Patching the system will not solve any of these problems, Mr. Speaker. It may hide some for a while and may quieten some of the unrest for a short period of time, but if we do not do something drastic soon unemployment will worsen, the welfare rolls will swell and Canada will become nothing short of a banana republic, supplying raw materials to multinational corporations. I do not think the Canadian people want that type of country and will not tolerate this type of approach. If we do not change direction democratically, then perhaps some of our people will seek change in a different way. I am referring to what is going on in parts of the United States, in Ireland, in the Middle East, in Pakistan, where many people have chosen a different option. I do not want that to happen, and it is not necessary for it to happen. We must bring change in our country in a meaningful way that will satisfy the people.
I want to go back to the promises which the Prime Minister made in 1968. At that time, he talked a lot about participatory democracy. I think that phrase has come to haunt hon. members opposite. I do not think any one of them can say that in this country we have had participatory democracy. There has not been national participation in the process of government. Instead, we have had task force after task force and white paper after white paper. We have had study groups. Now, there are to be white papers on white papers and task forces to study what other task forces have not studied.
Speech from the Throne
The Prime Minister thinks that participatory democracy is the process whereby the Prime Minister's office and not the people, not Members of Parliament and not even the cabinet, decides what must be done. I think you will find evidence of this contention in the speeches made in the last few months by the hon. member for Duvernay (Mr. Kierans) and the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) after they had left the Trudeau cabinet. To me, participatory democracy means allowing people to make decisions that affect their lives. To me, it means more than just listening to people; it means involving them in a meaningful way. It means more than elections every four years; it means listening to farmers, workers, small businessmen and young people, and asking what they want to do in evolving policies that affect them. That is not happening at all, under this Prime Minister. Instead, the Prime Minister's attitude towards certain groups, such as the Lapalme workers, has been made well known. To the Lapalme workers he said, "Manger de la merde". That is the type of insult the Prime Minister has aimed at the workers.
And what did he say to the western farmers? He said, "Why should I sell your wheat?" On one occasion he is alleged to have said, "You are quite wealthy, because I see $20,000 tractors out here." This is the type of attitude he has displayed towards farmers. And what has he done to help unemployment? At an elaborate, upper-middle class dinner in Toronto, he said that there are lots of jobs in Canada for those who want them. That has been his attitude towards the unemployed. When welfare recipients in Hamilton became too militant, the grant given to them by the Department of National Health and Welfare was cut off. That is not participation. Yet many people thought there would be participation when the Prime Minister took office in 1968.
The Opportunities for Youth program is an example of how this government operates. Even under that program, participation is limited. First of all, the program excludes non-students. It excludes the young people of this country. We know that in January of this year over 13 per cent of our young people between the ages of 14 and 34 were unemployed. They should be participating in a program like this, but they are not. According to the government's own sources, participation in the program has been confined to middle class students, and mostly upper-middle class students. They are the ones who are involved in Opportunities for Youth. If your father's bank account is big enough to support you at university, you can get a job under Opportunities for Youth. That is the type of participation this government has had in mind for the last several years. We know that some can participate, but the participation is primarily confined to the wealthy people of this country and to the multinational corporations. I suggest, with respect, that the government listens to those corporations.
I cannot help but remember a statement recently made, by Mr. Rankin, I believe, the president of the fund raising group of the Liberal party in Ottawa. He talked about 95 corporations which are giving funds to the Liberal party. I think the Liberal party probably listens to these corporations, and listens carefully. Why has there been a delay in the announcement regarding foreign ownership policy? Why has proposed legislation dealing with campaign funds been shelved? I wonder, Mr. Speaker. Perhaps

February 24, 1972
Speech from the Throne
these 95 corporations are exerting pressure. Perhaps they do not want the government to announce its policy regarding foreign ownership. Perhaps the government does not want the public to know about the people who contribute campaign funds to various political parties. Perhaps the Liberal Party wants to fill its campaign coffers first before making such announcements. After all, the party would not want to bite the hand that feeds it. That is the way the system in this country works.
I also want to know how much some of these corporations that obtain tax concessions and tax write-offs "participate". One way of finding out who "participates" in this way is by looking at the tax laws of our country. You can find out about the type of country you have if you analyze its taxation system. I have some statistics before me which tell a good deal of the story. Over the last ten years, one finds that different companies have been paying different rates of tax on their profits. Gas and oil companies in Canada, most of which incidentally are foreign owned, in the last ten years paid taxes on only 5.7 per cent of their profits in Canada. Mining companies in the last ten years paid taxes, on average, on 13 per cent of their profits and retail merchants, who are at the other end of the scale, paid taxes on 90 per cent of their profits. The man with a small business paid a great deal of tax, yet gas and oil companies, most of which are multinational corporations, paid taxes on only 5.7 per cent of their profits. There you see "participation". It is "participation" by companies like Shell Oil, Gulf, IBM, Parsons and Whitmore, and others like them. That is not the type of participation that my party wants or that the people of Canada want.
One can see the same sort of "participation" behind the recent cabinet shuffles. We know that Bay Street and big business were not too happy about the competition bill and certain amendments to labour statutes being considered. The former minister of consumer and corporate affairs and the former minister of labour were removed from their positions. In their places were appointed ministers more acceptable to the business community. If that is participation, it is not the type of participation or double standard that my constituents or members of my political party want.
The second great promise that the Prime Minister made in the 1968 election campaign was the promise of the just society. That, too, has come to haunt hon. members opposite. As I suggested when talking about taxation, the just society benefits the wealthy of this nation. It benefits the multinational corporations. This is serious, and affects many people in Canada. Many in my constituency, including farmers, the unemployed and elderly people, are very angry now when they hear talk about the just society. I was amazed to hear the hon. member for Bruce (Mr. Whicher) say, in beginning the Throne Speech debate, that the just society had arrived for the old people of Canada. The just society has arrived for the pensioners, according to him.

speechtext: Perhaps if you lift the rock, you will find it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I can only say to the hon. member for Bruce that there are pensioners I know in Yorkton and Melville who would like to confront him eyeball to eyeball

and tell him what they think. This is the type of statement which is making more and more people lose confidence in Canada, in the Canadian economy and in the Canadian political system. The best evidence that the just society is not here is the high level of unemployment in Canada. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) and the Prime Minister can say anything they want about how many jobs have been created and about the participation rate of the labour force. The fact remains that our unemployment rate is higher than that of any industrialized country. As we sit here this afternoon, nearly 7 per cent of the Canadian work force is unemployed. That is almost 700,000 Canadians. And this is not the whole story. We know that when the rate of unemployment is so high, there is hidden unemployment, people who have dropped out of the labour force, women who have not registered for employment but who would work if they had an opportunity to do so, people on welfare, people taking manpower courses, people on other courses the federal government is sponsoring. If all these were included there would probably be more than 800,000 people in Canada who would like to work today but who do not have jobs. It does not matter what we say in the House of Commons or what the Minister of Finance says about statistics. The stark reality is that many thousands of citizens in Canada are today walking the streets in sub-zero weather looking for jobs.
In 1971, an average of about 6 per cent of the working population were without employment during the year. It was not the same 6 per cent all the year round. Different people are out of work at different times of the year. If one counted all the people who were unemployed at various times during 1971 I believe one would find that upwards of two million people were unemployed in Canada at one time or another during the year. This affects us in many ways. It affects those who are unemployed. It affects their families directly. If all these people are included, one would find that five or six million people are directly affected by unemployment.
Any study will show that prolonged unemployment brings about many long-term disastrous results for the country. Unemployment of this magnitude creates a further core of permanently poor people, a further core of people who will be permanently unemployed even if the economy should return to operating at full capacity. Second, unemployment of this magnitude means that the economy is suffering, because it is not operating at full capacity as it would be if everyone was working. We are not producing the goods and services we could be producing if everyone had jobs. There is not as much demand within the economy as there would be if more people were getting incomes from jobs. Moreover, we cannot in these circumstances put an end to regional disparity.
The Department of Regional Economic Expansion was established on the basis of an economy operated at or near full capacity. This has not been the case and, as a result, the DREE program has been nothing but a total disaster.

The same can be said about the manpower program. It is not possible to operate a successful man-
February 24, 1972

power program when more people are being trained than there are jobs available for them, as is presently the case. The government conducted a job vacancy survey and from this we find that there are many fewer jobs available in Canada than there are people being trained to fill them. These are reasons for aiming toward a fully operating economy, an economy which provides full employment.
When we are talking about a just society we are not simply talking about the unemployed, we are not simply talking about the Indian people and the western farmers. We are talking about an attitude toward people of this country. Again, I wish to refer to the tax system in an effort to find out what the government means when it talks about a just society. We spent several months formulating a new tax policy. We spent several years on its preparation, going back to the Carter Commission and, finally, we came up with a new tax policy. This shows we do not have a just society in Canada, and that the term just society is very much of a farce.
Consider the cases of three men, each earning $10,000 a year. They have no dependants, yet they are all taxed differently because they earn their money in different ways or draw it from different sources. The first earns his money by working in a factory, or as a teacher. He will pay $2,285 in income tax. The second man makes his money from capital gains. He will pay only $844 in tax under the terms of the new bill. The third man makes all his money from dividends. He will pay only $193 in tax. This is the just society of the Liberal government. This is the just society which is being perpetrated upon the Canadian people. It is no such thing. It is just a laugh, and that is why it is coming back to haunt Liberal members who sit opposite.
The Minister of Finance told us that thousands of people who used to be liable for income tax will pay no income tax at all under the new tax bill. It is true the government did throw a few crumbs to the low income earner and that they now expect him to be happy. They increased the tax payable by those in the middle income range and lowered it as far as wealthy people are concerned. Again, I wish to use the cases of three single people to show hon. members what has happened. First, let us consider the case of a single man without dependants, earning $5,000 a year from wages or from working, say, as a farmer or as a teacher. His taxes will be decreased by $14 under the new bill. The taxes payable by a man without dependants who is making $10,000 a year will go up by $56 a year. Now, consider the case of a third man without dependants, a man who is a real pauper. He is living in poverty, making $100,000 a year. His taxes go down by $1,011.
