-and, of course, he would give a different interpretation than the one I would give, coming from a different background.
Then, there is the third great promise of the Liberal party. It is one hon. members opposite are very touchy about, national unity. This was one of the big issues upon which the Prime Minister campaigned. The Prime Minister undertook to unite this country, but in my opinion he has probably done less to unite Canada in three and one half years than any Prime Minister before him. One has only to consider what has happened since 1968. Since that year we have seen in Quebec the emergence of the Party Quebecois which won 24 per cent of the votes in the last election in the province. Spokesmen for the government can say what they like about this, but to me it is a clear indication that there is something drastically wrong about the way in which the Prime Minister has sought to solve the question of national unity. We have witnessed the emergence of the FLQ in Quebec, and everyone recalls the events of October, 1970. We have seen in western Canada the emergence of a number of organizations, respectable organizations, which are today questioning the value of our relationship with Ottawa and wondering whether we should seriously reconsider our role vis-a-vis Ottawa. They see Ottawa as a distant enemy, as an institution which is doing more harm than good in their lives. Without knowing very much about the maritimes, I understand that a similar situation is developing there, too.
I would hope that Canada could be a strong country, that Canada could be united. But this cannot be brought about by speeches alone or by constitutional conferences which fail to produce results. It must be recognized that we are dealing with regions which have special problems, special concerns, and individual aspirations. This, in itself, is a source of strength. The cultural mosaic of Canada is something which all of us can cherish. But before we can think in terms of a united country, all these regions must become equal partners. Today, because of the variations in the economy and between sections of society, this is just not the case. As the economy is presently oriented, industry naturally tends to locate in what is known as the golden horseshoe and in these circumstances, other regions of the country feel they are unwanted, that they are discriminated against. This is one of the reasons the Prime Minister has failed to achieve national unity; he has failed to tackle some of these basic problems which have arisen from coast to coast.
May I mention a few concerns of the prairie people? The role of the Prairies throughout the history of its development has been that of a supplier of raw materials, agriculture goods, and natural resources. As a result, we do not have much of an industrial base. In addition to this, tariffs and transportation costs have continued to discriminate against our future development. It has been pointed out many times that with an economy of this sort, which basically relies on raw materials, one has to export much of one's wealth, and this means that jobs that could be had in western Canada or in rural Quebec or the Maritimes are lost to us.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. As I was saying, each of the regions of this country has special problems that we must solve if Canada is to remain united in the future. In my part of the country we are exporters of raw materials and importers of manufactured goods. We export jobs as well as wealth.
In addition, in my part of Canada there is a good deal of concern felt about the future of the agricultural industry and the rural way of life that is being systematically destroyed. Today one sees farmsteads abandoned, the population of villages dwindling and communities that are turning into ghost towns. This must be stopped if the regions like the prairies are to have any confidence in the government at Ottawa. This country has a great future ahead of it, but to realize this future we must change direction and introduce some radical socio-economic measures. Our economy must be operated at full capacity and we must have a policy of full employment. We know how this can be done. It is the case in many other countries of the world today.
We must also tackle immediately the question of foreign ownership so that Canadians can control their own economy and destiny. We must redistribute power and wealth so that the ordinary people of Canada can have more say over what happens to their country, as well as their own destinies. Unless this is done, I do not know what the options are. But one thing I do know is that more and more Canadians might start looking for an alternate method of expressing themselves; and I do not want that to happen because we in Canada are capable of making the changes I have suggested in a democratic manner. We have the resources, we have the knowledge, and we have the technology to do so. All we need is a change in government policy that will redress our problems and change our priorities, so the average person will reap the benefits instead of the foreign corporations or the very wealthy.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Energy. Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to participate in this debate I should like first of all to extend my congratulations to the mover and seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. The mover, the hon. member for Bruce (Mr. Whicher), in his robust way, set forth his views on a wide breadth of subjects as they were dealt with in the Speech from the Throne and as they were dealt with by the hon. member. The hon. member does have an enviable faculty. Whether or not one agrees with him-and it would be an exaggeration to say that he is totally agreed with at all times in this House-he certainly has the faculty for commanding attention when he speaks.

Also, Mr. Speaker, to my friend, the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Lajoie) who also took part in the debate and supported the motion for an Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. I should like to offer my
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Boulanger)]
congratulations to the hon. member who hails from the historic region of Trois-Rivieres and who is part of a very distinguished line of representatives for this riding.
If on the one hand, my friend, the hon. member for Bruce (Mr. Whicher) is a veteran, a more experienced fighter who shows great wisdom, on the other hand the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres brings to this House all the originality and freshness of a new member and, in my opinion, he will certainly follow the very worthy tradition of this riding whose representatives have always been most clever.

It seems to me appropriate in entering this debate on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne to take the occasion to share with the House a few of my initial thoughts in approaching my new assignment as Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. The management of our earth resources is central to our economic and social well-being, to our national purposes, to federal-provincial relations, and is essential to our role in the international community.
Before proceeding with this question, however, I should like to join with the other hon. members who last week paid tribute to our colleague, the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Mr. Greene), for his conduct of this important portfolio which it is now my privilege to hold. I should like to join in that tribute and to say that it will be no small task to match his vigour and grasp of the perplexing issues, and the effort that he has made to bring all Canadians into the dialogue that will steer Canada's course into the 1970's and beyond. We are all looking forward to having our colleague with us again, his being able to share with us, both in the proceedings in public in this House and in private, the benefit of his wisdom and his incomparable good sense and humour.
To the serious and complex questions that are posed in my portfolio, there are really no simple answers. Canadians everywhere are concerned about the husbanding and developing of our resources, both for generations present and yet to come. It is clear that alternative courses can have consequences that would range across the broad spectrum in the future character of Canada as a whole, and many of its provinces and regions in particular.
To cite some of the complex, indeed critical, issues in the mineral and energy economy I would name the following: first, the orderly development of the resource base and the expansion of domestic and foreign markets; second, capital availability and issues relating to ownership and control; third, taxation policies. Fourth, there are major problems requiring new policies in the Arctic frontier and in the ocean frontiers off our two shores. Fifth, there is the question of economic growth and the establishment of environmental quality standards; sixth, the serious question of the need to integrate energy supply and demand patterns and to achieve reasonable energy costs; seven, the establishment of viable coal and uranium industry development; eight, the creation of transportation systems at realistic costs; and finally, but not least, the stability of communities that are dependent on the resource industries for the well-being of their people and the future of their children.
February 24, 1972

These and other problems have brought into sharp focus the need for the federal and provincial governments as well as industry to play a closer and more effective role in our resource development as an urgent matter of national interest. There is increasing acceptance of the interdependence of our respective roles and the clear fact that national policies, to be effective, must be the result of our combined experiences, our shared purposes and our common needs.
We at the federal level need to hold talks with the provinces to ensure that we have a thorough understanding of their views on resource management. It has been for the purpose of establishing such effective liaison that I have already met with Premier Lougheed of Alberta and will be seeing Premier Regan of Nova Scotia and Premier Hatfield of New Brunswick in the near future.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I would be delighted to see the hon. gentleman at any convenient time. As the son of a New Brunswicker, I look forward to seeing another distinguished immigrant from my father's province. There is no doubt that the provinces, as the owners of much of our mineral and energy wealth, are now playing and will continue to play a central role in the framing of national policies for resources. I believe we can find ways for them to contribute to the development of international negotiating positions, though the responsibility for these positions must always remain ultimately the responsibility of the Government of Canada.
We must make ourselves aware of their concerns, and they of ours. We need to take their concerns into consideration and, to the extent possible, choose approaches and policies that reflect these interests.
As outlined in the Speech from the Throne and I quote: -a continuation and strengthening of government-industry relations is necessary in order that such areas of challenge as environmental impact and the increasing demand both within Canada and abroad for resources and energy be fully addressed.
I have had an initial meeting with the representatives of the oil industry at Calgary and intend to spend much more time with the representatives of that industry, with the expectation that the National Advisory Committee on Petroleum and the National Advisory Committee on the Mining Industry formed by this government will provide a growing avenue of co-operation between industry and government.
The Speech from the Throne deals in some detail with the importance of international markets for our products and Canada's resources will continue to occupy an important place in our relationships abroad. The government has recognized this relationship over the past year or two when missions abroad have sought to extend our influence and promote a better understanding of resources and policies affecting them in Australia, Japan and Europe. Later this year, I hope to lead a mission to China in returning a visit paid earlier this year by that country to Canada which had a coast to coast look at our mineral and metallurgical industries in operation. Of particular importance in this field, of course, are the relations
25020-15J
Speech from the Throne
between Canada and the U.S., a subject that I will discuss in just a moment.
Speaking in general terms, there is a very real need to accelerate reviews of policies affecting minerals and energy and to achieve a consensus on the thrust of resource policy for the 1970's. These are needed to help ensure that our long-term approach as well as shorter term decisions are formulated in the best interests of all Canadians and to realize optimum national benefits from our resources. I hope to bring statements of these policies to the House this year.
I would add that resource policy must complement broader policy concerns for industrial strategy. It must provide improved social-economic security. It must provide improved performance of the domestic economy. It must represent an effort for expanded and diversified exports. It must emphasize the need for social sensitivity in northern development and, above all, it must emphasize the greater participation of Canadians in the decisionmaking process on problems and opportunities facing the nation in the 1970's. If the hon. member will allow me the privilege, I will be glad to entertain a question from him after I have put my argument.
A delicate balance must be maintained between the economic growth required to sustain a viable resource sector and the environmental impact of all aspects of resource discovery, development, transportation and marketing. The quality of the demand for energy must be assessed as well as the supply, and the tremendous capital requirement needed for all energy activity. What will be sought over the months ahead will be a blending of individual resource policies with national strategies to achieve as effective a balance as possible. Certainly, a set of blanket solutions will never adequately cope with our problems.
I would like to say a few words about the earth sciences. It is of crucial importance to have the facts of a situation before acting on it, and one of the prime responsibilities of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources is to provide the Canadian public with the essential information on the earth beneath our feet, which will allow Canadians to make wise decisions on how we live on it, play on it, exploit it, or preserve it for the future. Scientists in my department view the earth in its four dimensions: first, vertically, determining its properties from the surface to the central nickel-iron core; second, horizontally, from the Atlantic to the Pacific continental margins; third, from the U.S. border to the high Arctic, and, fourth, from the earth processes of the present time to those which folded our landmass and formed our ore deposits several billion years ago. From this perspective of information and understanding, they seek to provide us, policy makers and public alike, with unique insights for the future habitation and enjoyment of our Canadian landmass.
They tell us the size and shape of our landmass; they describe its natural textures and man's impact on them. From the days of the lone surveyor and his pioneering explorations in our frontier areas we are moving into the satellite age, with earth resource satellites such as ERTS monitoring our changing land surface every 17 days. Our scientists not only describe the land surface, but its subsurface as well. Through the national seismological ser-

February 24, 1972
Speech from the Throne
vice they monitor earthquakes and nuclear explosions alike, satisfying man's curiosity by defining the properties of the earth's inaccessible interior and, at the same time, providing the public with insights into the detection of nuclear explosions and their possible effect on Canada, or on the earthquake risks which must be considered in building and engineering construction.
The national geomagnetic service defines the changing magnetic field over Canada and the movement of the north pole, thus providing the essential information for navigation by compass across Canada. The geologists provide the key insights on where our resources are, how much we have, and whether they can be exploited. Simultaneously, they seek to generate new employment in declining mining communities, to assess the terrain impact of pipelines and engineering construction, and to advise on the potential resource loss when land is used for such alternate purposes as parks and hydro-electric power generation.
As many of my colleagues are aware, the 24th International Geological Congress and similar congresses in the fields of photogrammetry, cartography and geography will convene this summer in Montreal and Ottawa. They will involve more than 10,000 scientists from approximately 100 countries. 1972 is being hailed as Earth Sciences Year in Canada. The government of Canada has recognized the significance of these events through a series of commemorative postage stamps, to be issued during the year; and schools and universities across the country are undertaking special classroom and outdoor projects emphasizing the earth sciences.
With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I will quote from a recent statement by His Excellency the Governor General: Our nation's vastness, and the great variety of its physical structures and resources have made the earth sciences particularly important in the development of our country. Those knowledgeable in this field have been and remain, our explorers, helping to uncover the riches of the earth and teaching efficient management and conservation of those resources.
This government recognizes that the performance of our resource and energy industries has been a basic building block in the growth of Canada's national wealth, opening new frontiers, accumulating capital for re-investment, enhancing the scientific and technical skills of Canadians, and accounting for a useful export surplus. The maturing of these industries and their importance to the economy suggests the critical part they will play in furthering the development of other economic sectors as well as the quality of life for all Canadians.
I want to spend the few remaining minutes at my disposal in this debate to cover some of the problem areas of concern to us in the management of our resources. Canada has been and remains one of the most favoured nations in the world in so far as the availability of energy is concerned. We are the second largest per capita consumer nation and the sixth in total energy consumption. In recent years the component cost of fuel in most industrial activity has remained in the area of 4 to 5 per cent. We cannot automatically assume that we will always be in such a favourable supply position.
Much of our early industry was based on low cost hydro-electric energy. We are fast running out of economic sources of supply and the large potential projects that

remain are subject to considerable environmental and capital requirement concerns. Accordingly, we are as a nation increasingly turning the thermal electric generation, either convential or nuclear, and in these fields we must maintain lower fuel costs and achieve more efficient generation techniques if we are to continue to have a lower electric energy cost than most competing industrial nations.
Our nuclear research program and our assistance to electrical general and transmission research at such facilities as Hydro Quebec's Electric Research Institute will help realize these efficiencies. The uranium industry currently faces an over-supply position accompanied by depressed world prices and a consequent lag in exploration activity. On the other hand, current known uranium resources are fully committed near the end of this decade and it is obvious that increased exploration will be needed, given the eight years of lead time required to bring new deposits into production. Over the past year officials of my department have met with representatives of both consuming and producing countries to assess this situation and determine measures to stimulate this activity. We have been in consultation also with representatives of this very important industry in Canada and we hope to be tabling during this session a revised uranium and thorium bill.
I have already referred to the importance of our relations with the United States in the resources field. Our starting point in this relationship is that Canada and this government will continue to bargain hard to get access to markets for resources which have been further processed in Canada to the highest degree possible and to sell them at the best opportunity prices. At the same time, we should all bear in mind that Canada does not have a monopoly in most of these export-oriented resource industries and cannot expect, therefore, to lever massive advantages in terms of price or access to markets merely by sitting back and waiting for foreign buyers to come pounding on our door. Our policies must reflect a studied appreciation of the resources which may from time to time be available for export as clearly in excess of our own requirements and we must know our own needs. One of Canada's energy policy objectives is to ensure adequate and dependable sources of supply at reasonable costs. To this end the government is moving in a systematic way in the development of an inventory of our resources of oil, gas, coal and uranium.
Our trade relations in these matters with the United States will be among the most sensitive and important in coming months. The question of access to markets raises immediately the United States embargo on uranium, for example, a position that must surely be altered if the United States is to supply the needs of its industry toward the end of the decade.
In another area we are moving closer to the goal of full and unimpeded access to United States markets for oil and gas produced in Canada which is clearly surplus to domestic security and commercial requirements. In this connection, of course, one of the most important issues that has been before the House in the recent past has been the question of the west coast tanker route proposed by
February 24, 1972

the United States. My colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) has made clear in the House, and the government in an aide-memoire sent to Washington last August stated in the strongest possible terms Canada's reservations with respect to the ecological and other hazards of movement of oil by tanker from Alaska, down the west coast and through Puget Sound to northwestern United States refineries.
The recent report of the United States coastguard dealing with the potential dangers of such an adventure has only served to reinforce the view that all possible alternatives ought to be given serious study before any unilateral action is taken. In this regard we have made clear, with the government's Guidelines to Northern Pipelines of August, 1970, that we welcome applications to build oil or gas pipelines from Alaska through Canada in a land bridge to the continental United States.
I should here comment that a very effective program of co-operation between government and industry is one reason studies have proceeded to a point where we feel that we will be in a position within a year to receive and consider applications for northern pipeline construction. This co-operation should serve as a model for other government-industry relationships.
On the difficult question of foreign ownership in the resource field members will recall the measures taken by this government to sustain Canadian control over our uranium industry and the successful manner in which my predecessor interpreted the will of this House that Home Oil should remain a Canadian company. Anyone concerned deeply about the future of Canada must acknowledge a very real concern about the foreign ownership or control of key resource industries. At the same time, however, it is important to appreciate fully the huge amounts of investment capital which will be required to maintain a viable resource sector that can, in turn, contribute so much to the development of an industrial strategy for a stronger Canada. I favour a pragmatic look at the advantages and disadvantages of any particular investment action proposed for our economy with foreign investment having the onus of demonstrating its contribution to our Canadian wellbeing and to the aspirations of Canadians.
In the months ahead, members of the House will have opportunities to take part in the debate on policies for husbanding and developing Canada's energy and mineral resources, particularly under the consideration of departmental estimates. In my view these questions which fall under my responsibility are among the most important questions to be decided by Canadians in this decade. I will look forward to the contributions of hon. members and of provincial governments, industry and Canadians generally as the government moves to form its policies in this vital area. Perhaps a good starting point would be to ask my hon. friend if he would like now to pose his question.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to have the privilege of participating in the debate on the Speech from the Throne and I should like to seize the opportunity to congratulate the mover and seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. The hon. members for Bruce (Mr. Whicher) and for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Lajoie) performed this task with much dignity.
I have read His Excellency's speech over and over again, and I have even taken the liberty of making a few comparisons with past speeches. My conclusion is that the 1972 Speech from the Throne was merely a repetition of previous efforts and that no doubt the results of the whole thing will be the same as we have already experienced, and no more.
In this document, the present situation is described as in a dream, but when the dream comes to an end and we fall back to earth we realize that the same malaise, the same problems are still with us.
I am now particularly thinking of the unemployed. It is well known that the unemployment picture in Canada remains critical. It is a real tragedy for those involved. Mechanisms and programs brought forward by the government with much fanfare of publicity to eliminate unemployment and regional disparities have proved inadequate.
There are more Canadians now having to do without essentials because they are or have been unemployed for a certain period during the past three years. We are therefore further from the promised just society than at the opening of this legislature's first session.
In the Speech from the Throne for the third session, which began in October 1970, the just society was mentioned as a remote objective. This year, it has been left out, no doubt because the objective was so remote it was lost sight of.
I personally believe that the long quotations and the bombast inserted into the Speech from the Throne are just vain words and window-dressing. And that is all the more true when we consider the treatment the unemployed are now subjected to.
I suppose that most other members, as I did, spent the parliamentary recess trying to palliate problems created by the Unemployment Insurance Commission. That is why I should like to deal with the matter right away.
At the opening of this session, opposition members called for a review of the present situation, but in vain. It

seems that the government is unwilling to face a situation which it knows to be bad, or is unaware of it.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Perrault) endeavoured, during the oral question period on February 18, to minimize the situation by saying that a mere 1 per cent of benefit payments were delayed. I do not know what criteria he used to establish such percentage or where he got his statistics, but I will not ask him to prove his assertions, lest I would again upset the computer and delay the issuance of benefits.
I myself had the opportunity of asking for the revision of numerous files. Some of those cases have been solved. But a great many cases remain outstanding and they are not recent either. Some of these applications were filed in September, October and November 1971, and I notice that applications resulting from illness are usually those which lead to the longest delays in the issuance of benefits.
I am under the impression that the personnel entrusted with this service is inadequate and that in some cases the files are lost so that it becomes necessary to ask the applicants for new medical certificates, thus further disrupting the orderly operation of the administration.
In a particular case, a young man had filed an application in early December. After waiting a month and a half, he called me to explain his problem. I submitted the case to the UIC and eight days after asking for a revision of that file, an official informed me that the pay center had asked for photocopies of the decisions of the computer. Now even the computer goes wrong.
Another person, who stopped working for the same reason on August 23, 1971 and who resumed work more than two and a half months ago is still waiting for his benefits, and this after having produced four medical certificates. In other cases, income tax was unfairly deducted before the law came into force.
In some cases, they do not manage to trace back the contributions of the claimants who have to make further calls on their former employer. I even had to call employers to ask them to be kind and please produce a new certificate.
I could give scores of similar instances, but what is the use, when facts are being distorted and all the errors attributed to the claimants.
Last January 26, I received a letter from the Department of Labour informing me that in all pending cases, where it would be found that the settlement of a claim would be delayed through administrative inefficiency, benefits would be paid within the next 72 hours. It was also suggested that all claims submitted before December 1, 1971 would be reviewed within the next ten days, and that a decision would be taken.
Following this, I did not find any improvement and on February 15 the office of the Minister of Manpower and Immigration issued a communique stating that all claims for benefits in arrears had now been settled.
Since then, his parliamentary secretary has confirmed that the situation would become normal again during the month of March. Was he expecting the unsettled claims to disappear with the melting snow?
February 24, 1972

Mr. Speaker, what I find odd in all this is that I received no complaint from officials of other departments to the effect that their pay cheque was in arrears. I never had to complain that my own cheque, which I receive on the last day of each month, was late. I find it strange that it has been possible to organize a very efficient accounting system in all other departments, so that everybody be paid on time whereas complaints have been piling up for the past six months at the Unemployment Insurance Commission.
It seems to me it should have been possible to foresee the surplus of work that would result from the application of the new act and to get ready for it.
Please note that my criticisms are not aimed at the civil servants who do the best they can and who are even willing to do their utmost that their fellow citizens' claims might be met equitably.
To my mind, the problems stem from the administrative procedures adopted by high level bureaucrats in the Unemployment Insurance Commission who failed to foresee the problems that might crop up after centralizing the offices in the major centres.
Today we reap what was sowed five years ago by people who suffered from delusions of grandeur.
I see only one quick solution and I would ask the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Mackasey) and his parliamentary secretary to make note of it. The claims that are pending should be transferred to information offices where the reasons for the delay would be considered in the presence of the claimants. Some will say that this procedure could be expensive but, in my opinion, it would be less expensive and more efficient than the present one, because it would reduce the number of phone calls on the part of officials and claimants with regard to the same case.
I know that it is boring to hear the same things over and over, and others have said these things before me, but one must understand that it is worse for the claimant who has been waiting for two months and even longer for the cheque to which he is entitled and which he needs. If only this money came from taxes! But no! This money comes from a common fund to which both workers and employers contribute.
As to the problem of unemployment itself, I have referred to it at the beginning of my speech and, as far as I can see, there is nothing new in the Speech from the Throne indicating that it will be solved shortly. In this regard, we shall have to be content with dreams, as is the case with the Speech from the Throne.
In that famous document, one reads:
-events in Canada and elsewhere have continued to demonstrate the turbulence of this age of changing values and shifting attitudes.
I wonder to whom those words are addressed, if not to the successive governments we have had in the past 50 years.
Considering that Canadians have to pay $5 billion, for interest only on federal, provincial, municipal and school debts, with the blessing of this federal government and its predecessors, I say that it is not among the people that one must look for those changing values but right here.
Speech from the Throne
Those $5 billion distributed to the people would mean $275 per year for every man, woman and child. For an individual worker who works 40 hours a week, 50 weeks a year, that would mean 14 cents per hour, while for the married worker with three children, it would mean 70 cents an hour.
I think it would be needless to seek elsewhere the reasons for the increases in prices we have known these last few years. No matter what the income and the direct taxes of a person, most taxes are hidden indirect taxes, that is to say they are added to the price paid by the consumer in its everyday purchases.
That is confirmed by the report of the Senate Committee on poverty, which states that 56 per cent of an annual income under $2,000 goes in taxes.
Further on in the Speech from the Throne, we read the following:
Economic security is one of the most effective forces which to conquer social isolation.
But who contributed to the creation of economic insecurity and social isolation in Canada? Is it not the system that gets us deeper and deeper into debt every day and keeps the Canadian people in poverty by depriving them of half their income-even more, sometimes-so as to pay interest to those who hold the power to create money? Do we not see here again that values are being upset and minds giving way to instability?
Imagine! We must ask private interests permission to use the production created by our people. If that is not unsteadiness of mind, I wonder what it could be.
Again in the Speech from the Throne, we read this:
We in this place have a special responsibility to help bring these goals and those hopes within reach, to make real the Canada of which our forefathers dreamed: a land so large that some of it will remain always serene and unspoiled; a society which believes in the dignity of every single individual; a community which husbands its resources and shares them justly among this generation and those to follow;
How magnanimous, Mr. Speaker! One would think that we are in a monastery. There are a number of questions that we should ask ourselves. If total public and individual debts in Canada top one hundred billion, can it be said that our heritage has been wisely managed, and that the sharing is still equitable? Is human dignity being respected when, as this is actually done in Quebec, widows are forced to travel 50 miles and more to go and get a poor little welfare cheque of $5, when it cost her perhaps $6 and $7 for taxi fare to go to that office? When the young fellow who has been told: Go to school and learn something, and your future will be bright, is offered starvation wages when he does graduate from school, is this sharing and respect for human dignity?
Let us take the case of widows and people under 65 who do not draw old age security benefits and who are unemployed. Are these people getting their fair share, they who have been working for many years and who now find themselves unemployed because of sickness or age? What are we waiting for to lower to 60 the age of eligibility for old age security?
And yet over the past years, these very people have entrusted their confidence in the country's management.

February 24, 1972
Speech from the Throne
They have worked hard to make Canada the best country in the world. They have sacrificed themselves to give their country sons and daughters. They had them educated at the price of many sacrifices to get what? A country in debt and to be tenants in a country inherited from their parents and which they have improved themselves, to be proletarians within an economic system which gives the highest priority to machinery and money. And yet other countries with an average income less than ours are already granting old age security to their senior citizens aged 60 or more. Why not Canada?
This is where this country's administration has been leading us. There will still be junior civil servants, planning technicians and economists paid by the system to devise more programs which will give rise to more problems and drive us even faster in to bankruptcy. Wellmeaning people are being mislead by those programs and this bureaucracy, so much so that everybody is at a loss. As it happened when they were building the Tower of Babel, short and long term programs are being set up which are leading nowhere. And yet our citizens are caught in it and work hard at the tower. The workman does his best to patch up the cracks which have shown up over the years while the graduate works at adding additional steps to the tower to have it rise even higher.
In a different field, the Speech from the Throne stated and I quote:
A major factor in the strength of the Canadian economy is provided by exports. The Government will pursue vigorously the initiatives it has taken throughout the world to develop and maintain Canadian markets. Those advantages already gained by ministerial missions to other countries will be enlarged in a number of ways. One of these will involve the provision of better credit facilities.
This is another masterpiece. I wish that our missions sent abroad for granting interest-free loans would get lost and visit Canada to obtain information on regional needs and give Canadians the same kind of loans they make to foreign countries.
If such missions have been so successful in the past in foreign countries, why not try the experience here in Canada? Our people are no dumber than people in other countries, and the missions might prove just as successful. If so, they might intend to continue in the same manner.
I have a suggestion for the minister in charge of housing (Mr. Basford) in this regard. Why not start activities in the field of construction? We have already financed an interest-free loan in Great Britain in order to persuade the British to purchase Canadian materials for building their homes. I should be quite interested to see what the results would be in Canada.
However, one thing we are not short of now is needs. Moreover, this field is labour-intensive and material-consuming. It is one of our economy's most important sectors and could provide even more jobs.
We now have a shortage of housing, and the height of foolishness, Mr. Speaker, in my province, the province of Quebec, is that they are preventing construction workers from practricing their trade, subject to a fine, by making a working permit mandatory. That is another instance of upside down values and true mental instability.
To start this experiment, the minister responsible for housing could call on his colleague, the Minister of

National Revenue (Mr. Gray), to remove the 12 per cent sales tax on building materials. This would be a true step forward to help those who need housing and to create jobs.
Another way to assist the building industry would be to grant a subsidy on the interest paid upon the purchase of houses for low-income people. Instead, we accept through social welfare to pay for the cost of housing that is often above $100 or $125 per month. We do not want Canadians to become home-owners; we would rather let them be tenants, even if it is more expensive, Mr. Speaker. This is where our management of the country is leading us.
A few years ago, we granted other interest-free loans to Jamaica for the construction of sewage and water systems in the city of Kingston, the capital. Why could we not grant the same privilege to Canadian municipalities whose numerous programs gather dust on shelves for lack of funds or because the interest rates are too high?
The construction of sewage treatment plants would create jobs and simultaneously contribute to the fight against pollution. There is another field in which Canadian needs are tremendous. If extending credit facilities to other countries is a good thing, it might be time to check whether or not it might not also be so, here in Canada, before dashing right and left.
With regard to our exports, Mr. Speaker, obviously we must find new markets and keep those we already have. We have to import products that are manufactured here in Canada; I am thinking of agricultural products that have to be imported from tropical countries. Now, our exports help our balance of payments, but in spite of that, ti will be hard to convince us that we must export in order to survive. Nor do I agree with the economists who in every country in the world, preach that exports must be greater than imports, How, then, could all the countries in the world at one and the same time export more than they import? It is absurd to think that all countries could have a favourable balance of payments at the same time. Before exporting, it is necessary, in my opinion, to meet domestic demand, to fulfil the needs of the people for food, clothing, housing and public utilities.
Until such time as those objectives are met for the benefit of the people, we must ask ourselves questions and try and find out what is truly wrong in our country. Until we find means to cope with internal consumption and succeed in making use of the available manpower and factory potential, we will have to ask ourselves questions. The duty of management is to implement mecan-isms to ensure the welfare of the Canadian people.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I wish to point out an excerpt from the Senate Committee on Poverty Report where it is said that one Canadian out of four, which means five million Canadians, receives an income which is less than what is considered as the threshold of poverty.
This is a great challenge that management will have to take up as soon as possible, because the gap between poverty and affluence increases from day to day, as yvell as the number of destitute people. The number may double in five years. The challenge is a serious one, and we must face it.
February 24, 1972

Mr. Speaker, along with other Members of Parliament who have already spoken in this debate I, too, wish to commend the hon. member for Bruce (Mr. Whicher) for moving the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. If life in Canada is not quite as good and glowing as he would have us believe, it is certainly not as dark and dismal as some opposition spokesmen have contended. The hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Lajoie) delivered what I thought was an exemplary speech in seconding the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. His constituents have good reason to be proud of his performance. I think he did particularly well in drawing attention to the government's plans to take further steps to stimulate our economy. Effective measures in this area will contribute much to national unity and national pride. It is difficult to feel at one with other Canadians or to take delight in our national identity if economic circumstances separate some in an unhappy state of poverty and misery.
The hon. member for Bruce stated in his speech that Canada pays the highest old age pensions in the world. I am not able to refute that statement, and it may very well be true, but it seems to me to be quite beside the point. The point is, surely, that pensions almost always turn out to be inadequate if they are based upon a fixed number of dollars. The constant complaint of most people whose income depends upon a pension is that it seemed like a very comfortable sum when it was first set up, but shrunk to poverty level in purchasing power because of inflation.
A recurring term in the Speech from the Throne is that of "isolation". In the constituency which I represent, the electoral district of Thunder Bay, isolation is more than just a word-it is a daily reality for many people.-North of the CNR mainline, a great many of my constituents, native Indians of Canada, live in isolated reserves and settlements. Many of these native persons are now migrating into cities and towns and the result for them is a feeling of terrible alienation. The city is seen by them as a foreign land, owned and operated by white men. Social and sometimes even psychological disorientation sets in, and all too frequently this leads to serious personal problems for these people. Many Canadians see only these Indian people who have been stripped of all human dignity caused by severe cultural shock and it is sad but true that there is a tendency to judge all Indian people by these unfortunate souls with whom they come into contact.
Some communities have now set up what are called Friendship Centres for native people. For those who may not know, these centres are social service agencies which exist to administer programs to meet the evolving needs of all migrating native people. The Department of the Secretary of State presently provides small grants to assist these centres. I notice that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State is here. He knows my feelings about this, namely that the grants are much too small and that the centres which are in greatest need are not getting grants sufficiently large in proportion to those received by centres which are not doing the same job. For example, the Friendship Centre in Thunder Bay deals with people from all over the region and is called upon to
Speech from the Throne
bear correspondingly large costs for administration and programming. As for programming, the provincial government provides a somewhat larger sum of money but nevertheless, these friendship centres are today facing a financial crisis and find themselves unable to provide the quality of staff or the level of services that they would wish. Accordingly, I take this opportunity to call upon the government to adopt a reasonable policy of assistance to migrating native people, one which will include a much more generous measure of support for Friendship Centres.
On the same subject, that is, the isolation of native people, it is further necessary that steps be taken to improve the systems of communication and transportation among the scattered reserves and settlements in Northern Ontario. It is now possible to achieve this goal by relatively inexpensive means.
The Speech from the Throne proposes that the CBC be authorized to extend its services in a comprehensive fashion. Many of my constituents have no television or radio service at all. Others must tolerate very poor reception and most must content themselves with only partial service at best. For example, in nearly one half of my constituency, television viewers face a blank screen following the national news at 11:00 p.m.-there is no late evening television. I suppose that some here would argue this is not a drastic deprivation to be suffered, but if a person is a shift-worker and lives in a community which offers little else in the way of entertainment, a blank screen can be an annoyance of some consequence. There is a real demand for this service. Recently, a petition was posted in two stores in one small community and within a week 375 signatures were collected. The CBC is well aware of this gap in their service and I am pleased to say that steps are soon to be taken to correct this situation. We have now received such an assurance from the President of the CBC.
The hon. member for Bruce noted in his speech that his constituency has a second channel, an alternate TV service. There is not even a slight hope, Mr. Speaker, that my constituents will see the CTV network for many years to come. Therefore, although we may criticize the CBC for its less-than-perfect service and question its efficiency, although we may grumble about its programming, we do realize that if we did not have a publicly-owned broadcasting system in Canada, many Canadians outside the larger urban centres would enjoy neither television nor radio reception of any kind.
The Speech from the Throne also contained reference to seven new national parks created in Canada since 1968. One of these parks, Pukaskwa National Park, is located almost entirely within my constituency. It gave me great pleasure to participate in the official signing ceremonies, together with the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) and the Ontario Minister of Lands and Forests. Approximately 725 square miles in area, Pukaskwa National Park takes in some 50 miles of rugged Lake Superior shoreline. At its widest part, the park will span some 30 miles inland. The land is part of the Precambrian Shield, rugged in nature with numerous bays, beaches, rocky points and islands along the shoreline. In the interior of the park are numerous wild rivers,
230

Speech from the Throne
creeks with waterfalls, rapids and many small and large lakes.
In developing the park, the Indian people will be fully involved to ensure that important economic and employment opportunities are realized by them.
So far, I have been referring to the east end of my constituency around Lake Superior, near the towns of Marathon and White River. I should now like to move to the other end of my constituency, nearly 500 miles to the west. Here we find the energetic, progressive pulp and paper town of Dryden which now boasts a modern, paved airport capable of handling medium-range jetliners-this in a community of 7,000 people which serves a district that has about 15,000 people. In this area, the semi-isolation of being located along the Trans-Canada highway and on the CPR mainline, miles from anywhere, has now been shattered. To date, the federal government has spent nearly half a million dollars on the development of this modern municipal airport.
May I add that during the forthcoming election campaign, whenever it may be, on behalf of my constituents I extend an invitation to the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) and to the leaders of the opposition parties as well, to drop into Dryden as they jet back and forth across the nation trying to win votes. I can promise them all that a warm and friendly response awaits them.

The Speech from the Throne states that the government will continue to develop programs to strengthen secondary industry. I say to this government that the economic growth and development of Northwestern Ontario depends in large measure on lower freight rates. Freight rate incentives would assist this region to attract resource processing and manufacturing industries, as well as stimulating the existing primary and resource oriented sectors. Remote geographical location and low population density contribute to an inequality of opportunity, which we have always had to live with, but it seriously affects our ability to compete with other parts of Canada and abroad. Long haul distances significantly increase the selling price of goods and materials in the marketplace.
As most hon. members know, the pulp industry has suffered badly in recent years and prospects for 1972 do not appear much better. Pulp markets are in considerable oversupply and no realignment is in sight. Many one-industry pulp and paper communities are now living under the cloud of threatened lay-offs and even permanent shutdowns. The industry is, relatively speaking, labour-intensive; wages are reasonably good and working conditions are generally fair to good. My constituents have taken note of the generous treatment extended to prairie wheat growers with the recently announced two-price system. We approve of this and the assistance offered to the Canadian book publishing industry, but we want to know, in this government's design of a so-called "industrial strategy", what consideration is being given to

the pulp and paper industry. Hopefully, it is not a policy of assisting in the establishment of new mills while allowing older mills to close their doors, thereby causing the death of communities, with all the social waste involved as well as the dislocation of thousands of people.
The electoral district of Thunder Bay is a resource-rich region of Canada. I was pleased to hear this afternoon the speech of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald), and I should like to take this opportunity of congratulating the member for Rosedale on his recent appointment to this most important portfolio.

We are looking forward to his forthcoming visit, his non-political visit, to Northwestern Ontario to see some of the mines there in operation.
Mining is one of the big industries in Northwestern Ontario. It is a risky enterprise which helps to open up the north. It is true that this industry gets a special tax deal, and that under the new tax legislation it will continue to receive favourable treatment provided an investment is made in the first place. I note that periodically members of parliament from both sides of the House, and also would-be experts in the academic world, call for a fostering of job-intensive industries in preference to the resource industries. Usually, the people who advocate this policy as part of an industrial strategy come from large cities like Toronto or Montreal. I appreciate their sincerity in wanting to see many more jobs created quickly, and with that I have no quarrel. One problem is, of course, that fostering job-intensive industries means the continuing rapid growth of large urban centres, while the hinterland of Canada remains dormant. I suppose that ecological pantheists who equate God with nature may cheer at this prospect, but urbanologists must shriek with despair at the thought of cities expanding endlessly and relentlessly.
The fact is that we in the more remote areas of this country also want a part of the action. We resent very strongly undue exploitation of any kind, whether that exploitation is directed from Wall Street or Bay Street. What we want is an orderly, rational development of our resources, taking into account the wisdom of conservation and the necessity for environmental protection and preservation. Thus, we regard it as being callous indeed to say that there should be no development at all, little or no investment in resource industries.
The development of the Mattabi mine on Lake Sturgeon has given the little railroad and tourist town of Ignace a big lift. A town plan has been drawn up, and the building of many new homes offers the promise of the good life to these people in Northwestern Ontario without it being necessary for them or their children to migrate to the choking atmosphere of Toronto or some other large centre. There are other communities, such as Geraldton, Nakina, Armstrong and Beardmore, that look forward to the day when some of the mining exploration that has been going on for years around those towns leads to development, production and job opportunities, with the growth of these communities and their economies.
One of the characteristics of being a Canadian is having the ability to meet the challenges of living in a northern
February 24, 1972

environment, not in any simple, primitive condition, but in an advanced civilization in which we make use of the many tools and techniques of modern industry to provide for ourselves a high standard of living. We in the north want to share in these benefits.
On another subject, Mr. Speaker, the Speech from the Throne promises that parliament will have the opportunity to consider a new Canada Labour Code. One of the most controversial aspects of this proposed legislation has been the technological change provisions, which would provide the trade unions with notice of all significant technological changes and, in carefully defined circumstances, permit them to negotiate during the lifetime of an agreement provisions designed to assist employees in adjusting to the effects of technological change. The Canadian Chamber of Commerce has officially opposed these provisions, saying that they would jeopardize the economic well being of industry and Canadians generally.
There is another important and strong argument on the other side, however, and this counterview has been well expressed by the small Chamber of Commerce located in the little railroad town of Nakina, in my constituency. Recently, they took it upon themselves to write a letter to the national president of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce in which they took the opposite view to what their parent body has said about the proposed Canada Labour Code and the technological change provisions. I think the House should hear what they had to say, because what they said comes from first-hand experience. The letter reads:
Our small community has had two close brushes with "technological change" when the CNR attempted to run-through in 1964 and again in 1969. We know too well the results of such changes when not brought on with care and consideration of all things concerned.
If the CNR run-through had taken place-and we don't know that it still won't-it would have left Nakina with one-third fewer residents and the reduction of earning power by almost one-half. The result would have been fewer tax dollars coming into the town office, businesses would have had to cut staff drastically, with some merchants fearing they would have to fold, thus causing an even greater loss of employment.
Technological change is inevitable, but to do it in a haphazard way, not taking into account the employees and communities involved, is to seriously jeopardize our "economic well being". We believe that unions should have the right to stall change, if only until the signing of the next collective agreement, so that technological change may be bargained about sensibly and brought on smoothly by minimizing the adverse effects.
It is with these people that I will take my stand because I experienced this run-through threat in 1969. A former Member of Parliament from another party had this same experience in 1964. The point made in that letter is a good one. We hope the government will proceed with this part of the Canada Labour Code and see it through.

As a final point, Mr. Speaker, I note that the Speech from the Throne speaks of policies designed to promote tourism in Canada. Tourism is another important industry in Northwestern Ontario, and we welcome all efforts by the federal government which will further assist in its growth and development. It is most important,
Speech from the Throne
however, that the economic benefits from this industry accrue mainly to Canadians.
In this regard, hon. members may recall the stir and fuss raised by elected representatives from Northwestern Ontario concerning U.S. licensed aircraft operators flying sportsmen into our region and reaping rich rewards from our resources. They were profiteers of the worst kind from south of the border, taking all they could get and contributing nothing to either the regional economy or the national economy. As a consequence of the concern and activity of many persons in Northwestern Ontario over a protracted period of time, the air transport committee of the Canadian Transportation Commission in December 1970 placed restrictions on these U.S. licensed aircraft operators. They were permitted to make two traffic stops only, one at the customs port of entry and the other at a licensed base of a Canadian chartered commercial air carrier. We considered this to be a significant victory for Canada and Canadians but, alas, our hurrahs were shouted a little too soon.
In May of last year, an American operator, Frank E. Bohman of Minnesota, applied for a review of the order of the air transport committee. On August 27, the review board, despite strong arguments from elected representatives and various departments of the government of Ontario, amended its order governing U.S. carriers of fishermen and hunters into our region. Although some restrictions are still in effect, they are so watered-down that the only possible interpretation is that what we now have is another Canadian sellout. The efforts of those of us who spoke against Bohman and in defence of Canadian enterprise and our own resources were labelled by the Canadian lawyer representing this American profiteer as jingoists. When the economic history of Canada during the 70's is written, the infamous Bohman case may well be indexed under the heading of "Our National Shame". This, of course, was not a government decision. I recognize that. I had the impression, however, that the Canadian Transport Commission and the air transport committee existed for the wellbeing of Canada and Canadians. The Bohman case causes me to have second thoughts about that.
The Throne Speech debate is a good opportunity for all hon. members to comment favourably or otherwise about the times in which we live. Like artists, we take brush to canvas and paint our pictures, bright or dark. In reality, the scene is one of contrast, for as the Prime Minister said in his New Year's address to the nation, quoting the opening lines from Dicken's novel "A Tale of Two Cities"-"It was the best of times, it was the worst of times".
Horace Greely, in his "American Conflict", remarked that the illusion that times that were are better than those that are, has probably pervaded all ages. However, we see the picture of our times, this Parliament has a great deal of work to do for the betterment of our nation and for the well-being of its citizens.
