I propose to outline and comment upon the significance for Canadian publishers and the general public of Canada's non-adherence to the UNESCO agreement on the importation of educational, scientific and cultural materials, the Florence agreement, which has been operating since 1952.1 accept the fact that there is a certain risk in speaking about this issue because perhaps publishing and the distribution or free flow of knowledge is not usually expected to be a popular subject in the parliamentary sense. I want to acknowledge the help and interest of Mr. Paul Thomas, a parliamentary intern, in gathering a good deal of the data to support the remarks I make today. I am sure any of us who have had the privilege of having the assistance of parliamentary interns want to compliment the donor foundation for its generosity and want to say a special word for these young people who have added immeasurably to the zest and interest in the parliamentary process.
The main purpose of the agreement is to help fulfil a basic aim of UNESCO, as set forth in its constitution, "to promote the free flow of ideas by word and image". The agreement aims to reduce tariff and trade obstacles to the international circulation of educational, scientific and cultural materials, principally by means of contracting states forgoing custom duties on such materials. Many categories of printed materials are covered by the agreement, but the most important category is books. The United Nations lists 63 countries as applying the Florence Agreement. Unfortunately, our country is not among these.
Canada has not signed the Florence Agreement according to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp). In answer to a question of mine on June 30, 1971, as recorded at page 7510 of Hansard, it has not been considered to be in Canada's interest to abandon the
limited protection offered domestic producers against imports of certain educational, scientific and cultural materials, as long as important trading partners maintained barriers against Canadian exports of these materials. The minister went on to say that Canada's accession to the agreement was under continuous review. The principal non-tariff barrier to Canadian book exports is the United States manufacturing clause. In the U.S. Copyright Act the phrase "Manufactured in the United States" means that the type must be set, plates made, sheets printed and books or periodicals bound in that country. The manufacturing clause provides that any work in the English language that is first published in the United States must be manufactured there if United States copyright protection is to be obtained. This holds true regardless of the nationality or residence of the author.
Any English language work first published abroad, and written by a foreign author residing abroad, need not be manufactured in the United States if copyright protection is to be obtained. Thus, the clause has no effect on a Canadian writing in Canada and selling into the United States. For an American writing and publishing abroad, there is a limit of 2,000 imported copies on which copyright protection can be obtained. A new United States copyright law has been under consideration in Congress for several sessions. In the 90th Congress, bill HR 2512 would have eased the provisions of the manufacturing clause somewhat. For example, the requirement of U.S. manufacture would no longer apply where at least a substantial part of the work has been written by a foreign author or, under certain conditions, by an American residing abroad. Moreover, a violation of the manufacturing clause would not jeopardize, as it now does, the protection of non-publication subsidiary rights such as dramatic television and motion picture rights. This bill, however, has apparently not been acted upon in the present 91st Congress because the responsible Senate subcommittee is trying to untangle the copyright problems raised by cable television. Pending revision of the United States law, Canadian book sellers and printers have pressed successive governments to seek a special exemption in exchange, perhaps, for Canada's removal of duty on United States books.
Canada now levies a 10 per cent duty on imported books. The percentage is of the cost of the book. There is provision in the Custom and Excise Act for exemption of certain categories of books. Technical books, for example, are exempt from duty, but the act does not define this term; its application is left to customs officials. Curious anomalies arise because of the imprecision of the act. The book by Manchester, The Death of a President, was first classified as a biographical work, subject to the 10 per cent surcharge. Later, it was reclassified as history and became exempt. Books adopted on university courses are also exempt. If a book is sold to an educational institution, the bookseller may apply for a rebate, though many do not because of the time and red tape involved in dealing with the customs department.
Mr. Barry Britnell, Chairman of the Copyright Committee of the Canadian Booksellers Association, stated that practically all of Britnell's books come in duty-free, but partly because he takes the time to seek exemptions. As an explanation of the price differential between Canadian

February 24, 1972

and United States copies of books, the duty does not appear to be all that significant. While pricing policies vary, Mr. Britnell stated that some publishers spread their duty across all their books, non-exempt and exempt, so that the increase in price would be less than 10 per cent on any one book. Mr. Britnell felt that some publishers did use the duty as an excuse to maintain prices at levels slightly higher than warranted.
There are more important factors at work than the surcharge causing higher book prices in Canada. At various times the following factors have been of greater or lesser significance: higher distribution costs in a relatively sparsely populated country, costs of providing additional services, catalogues, promotion for imported books, the current exchange rates in some cases, provincial sales tax, financing difficulties of Canadian publishers, brokerage fees, and the schedule of discounts that a principal offers a Canadian agent.
I admitted at the outset that it is risky to discuss a subject like this, but I feel the issue perhaps is important enough to have it on the record. Perhaps following the comments I make, those in this field will be able to make some comments and criticisms of the proposals I make and the issue of the free flow of books in the world, so the adherence to the Florence Agreement will thus become an acceptable policy to the government of Canada.
The various sectors of the book business appear to be divided over the appropriate course for Canada to follow with regard to free trade in books. The Canadian Book Publishers Council on January 27, 1972 passed a resolution requesting the government of Canada to seek an exemption from the manufacturing clause in a revised U.S. Copyright Act as a stimulus to the unrestricted flow of books into the United States from Canada, as is presently the situation in the reverse direction. The members of the Canadian Independent Publishers Association headed by Peter Martin regard the CBP as effectively controlled by foreign subsidiaries of United States publishing houses and, therefore, insensitive to the issue of publishing Canadian materials. This group apparently regards the copyright issue as of minor importance compared to the more urgent issue of the survival of a Canadian book publishing industry.
The Canadian Booksellers Association takes the position that adherence to the Florence Agreement should follow the securing of an exemption from the United States manufacturing clause. There is a feeling in this group that the Canadian surcharge attempts to protect Canadian publishers in an ineffective manner by raising the price of United States books. This point is made in the brief by W. H. Smith & Sons to the Ontario Royal Commission on Book Publishing where it is stated:
This tax is levied on the supposition that it in some way supports the Canadian book industry. This is not so and we suggest that it should be removed. The funds raised by this tax are not reinvested in the industry, but go into the general revenue of the government. It does not positively assist the Canadian publisher. It simply makes American books more expensive and so the only loser is the Canadian purchaser and reader.
All three groups point out that Canadian international copyright law gives copyright protection to a foreign publisher wishing to sell his books in Canada, regardless of where they are manufactured. Thus, there is no economic
Speech from the Throne
incentive for a foreign published book to be made in Canada, even if it is a best seller with a volume that would be attractive to a Canadian manufacturer.
I should like to discuss for a minute some of the major problems of the publishing industry in our country, and then make some suggestions about that. Public concern about the survival of a Canadian publishing industry has been aroused by such recent events as the sale of two Canadian publishing firms to Americans; the announcement by McClelland & Stewart Limited of its financial difficulties and the decision of the Ontario government to provide $1 million in no interest debentures to avert the possible bankruptcy or sale of the company to American interests; the hearings of the Ontario Royal Commission on Book Publishing; the publication of the study of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce on "The Canadian Book Industry"; the warnings of the Davey Committee on the Mass Media about the declining health of the industry; and the criticisms from the industry that the federal government has made no plans to use the occasion of International Book Year, 1972 to stimulate interest in books and to launch a co-ordinated policy of support for Canadian publishing.
I should like also to refer to the recent revelation that the Secretary of State's (Mr. Pelletier) proposals to cabinet for assistance to Canadian publishing had apparently been considerably narrowed down within the cabinet, and, most recently, the announcement by the Secretary of State pending the development of the government's long term policies. The major problems of the book industry in Canada include: the high percentage of imported books consumed; the distribution problems encountered by Canadian publishers; the absence of a real Canadian presence in certain fields of publishing such as the mass paperback market and children's books; the difficulties faced by publishers in obtaining operating capital; the practice of Canadian libraries and educational institutions of dealing with foreign book distributors who have larger stocks but fewer Canadian titles; the limited export markets due to such factors as U.S. copyright law; and the peculiarities of a market served by French and English language publishing industries operating under different conditions, through different techniques, and, to some extent, with differing philosophies. Each of these problems will be discussed briefly, and then I will try to make some assessment of the government's recent proposals.
The ITC study of 1969 states that the Canadian book industry is made up of about 300 organizations publishing books and approximately 25 manufacturers whose principal activity is manufacturing books. Of these, about 100 publishers account for virtually all books authored or adapted and manufactured in Canada.
Of the estimated $222 million worth of books at publisher's sales value consumed by Canadians in 1969, 65 per cent were imported books, 25 per cent were Canadian published and manufactured books, and 10 per cent were adapted books manufactured in Canada. On a language basis, 52 per cent of books sold in English Canada are direct imports, 14 per cent are adaptations, and only 34 per cent are produced and published in Canada. Of these, 80 per cent are published by foreign controlled firms, so

February 24, 1972
Speech from the Throne
that only 5 per cent of all English language books sold are authored, published and manufactured by Canadian controlled publishers. Only 30 per cent of the French language books are locally produced. I apologize for these statistics, but I think that in the context of these remarks it might be interesting to have them in some form on the record.
Of the $144.8 million worth of imported books consumed in Canada in 1969, 80 per cent came from the U.S.A. Since 1966 the volume of U.S. books imported has risen by 57.6 per cent, a scant 8 per cent and 7 per cent respectively come from Great Britain and France; about 58 per cent of the imported books were distributed by Canadian publishers, and the remaining 42 per cent were sold directly to Canadian wholesalers and institutions.
The ITC study also notes that the value added by book manufacturing and publishing accounted for .09 per cent of the 1969 Canadian gross national product. The contribution is approximately one third of the contribution made by the book industries in leading book publishing countries, and that fact might well be underlined. During the year 1969, the Canadian book industry exported only $5.5 million worth of books. Destination of exports is not given, but presumably a high percentage goes to the United States.
The English language industry has several large firms, but is principally dominated by a number of small firms having less than $2 million sales volume and relatively low capital investment. Larger firms earned more money and the small firms were in the vulnerable position of earning very marginal returns. Canadian publishers make most of their profits by acting as agents for foreign publishers. Canadian books tend to lose money. According to Paul Audley, Macmillan of Canada has been instructed by the British parent to cut back on its publication of Canadian works for precisely this reason. The respondents to the ITC survey cited capital availability as the greatest advantage of an agency relationship. In an argument familiar to the broadcasting situation, it is argued that imports in effect subsidize less popular Canadian books.
Canadian publishers also made profits by printing long runs of standard school text books. For the ITC sample, textbooks represented 65 per cent of total sales in English, somewhat lower than in the French language sector. This source of revenue is being undermined by increased competition from foreign sources through the "buying around the agent" practice. This involves placing institutional orders directly with foreign distributors, who carry large inventories, have sophisticated processing procedures, and buy in bulk at reduced prices. Often this means that institutions are buying American or French books. Moreover, there is a general reluctance among foreign publishers to modify their textbooks to suit Canadian conditions. This is a very urgent point.
Canadian owned publishers produced only 46 per cent and 45 per cent of Canadian elementary and secondary textbook sales respectively. I do not suppose many people in Canada are aware of this fact. Only 9 per cent of post secondary textbooks were produced by Canadian owned publishers. Ryerson Press and W. J. Gage Limited, both recently sold to American firms, accounted for a great part of this textbook production, and now there are only
[Mr. Fairweather.)
two Canadian owned houses that do any significant amount of textbook publishing.
This is a somewhat long and boring speech about an interest that has come to me because I reviewed a book once published in the U.S.A. on the life of an American ambassador, Chester Bowles. The sale price in the United States was $12.95 and in Canada $18.75. I commented on this differential and I have had a flood of information from interested people since. So, I am afraid, Mr. Speaker, you have to put up with this; I am sorry.
Two areas where the Canadian presence in publishing is virtually non-existent are children's books and popular paperbacks. If any of my colleagues have tried to pick up at an airport a popular Canadian paperback when they are going to and from their constituencies, they know the difficulty of which I speak. According to Paul Audley, less than five children's books were published by Canadian firms last year. In the popular paperback field, distribution arrangements that permit monopoly control on outlets to arise means that almost all paperbacks sold in drug stores, department stores, newsstands, airports, etc. are foreign titles, mostly American. The problem of access to the shelves is a recurring theme in the testimony of Canadian publishers to the Ontario Royal Commission on book publishing.
There are several reasons for the paucity of Canadian children's books. Most children's books are sold in department stores and supermarkets, so Canadian publishers again have difficulty finding outlets and owners buy from foreign jobbers. Successful children's books have become colourful, often with expensive illustrations, so that long runs are necessary to offset costs. The CBPC estimated that over 50,000 copies sold are needed to recover costs, and even then recovery is slow.
I want to discuss some obstacles to export, then make a suggestion or two, and then sit down. Presumably, an industry with a small, sparse density market would seek export sales. There are several obstacles to exports by Canadian publishers beyond the copyright problems with the United States already mentioned. There is little demand for non-fiction trade books published by Canadians because the subjects are of little interest outside of Canada. The most popular Canadian authors often have separate United States and United Kingdom publishers and when a joint run with another publisher is possible, the printing is usually done outside Canada.
Manufacturing costs of books are generally higher in Canada, which in turn is reflected in higher prices. The risks involved in entering other markets and the costs of promotional and distribution facilities are too great for Canadian publishers with low profit levels. It is unappealing to those publishers' agents who are content to profit from being importers.
Traditional financial institutions have shied away from providing loans to publishers because of the uncertain nature of the business. This point was repeatedly made by publishers to the Ontario Royal Commission on Book Publishing when it was stated that long-term development loans at reasonable rates of interest were needed to allow for the development of Canadian books. This financing difficulty is most acute for the smaller, new houses which
February 24, 1972

are often publishing the most interesting Canadian material. Foreign-owned houses are often a part of a conglomerate with powerful financial backing. Credit is easier for them to obtain.
Ironically, McGraw-Hill partly financed its takeover of Ryerson Press through funds borrowed from Canadian banks.. When foreign-owned publishers handle Canadian books, they are often able to offer the authors sizable advances, the assurance of a larger market and better promotion and distribution. The Canadian houses often lose their authors and revenue.
The Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) announced on February 11, 1972, a five-point assistance program for the book industry: allocation of $500,000 in the fiscal year starting April 1 for bulk purchases of books by Canadian authors, which will be donated by federal agencies to public libraries in Canada and abroad; Canada Council grants totalling $1 million in the coming fiscal year for the publication of books by Canadian authors, double the amount spent last year; grants of $215,000 to finance English and French translations of Canadian books, an increase of $100,000 over last year; a $500,000 program by the trade department to open Canadian book distribution offices in the United States, Britain and Europe and to extend Canadian participation in international book fairs; contracts to commercial publishers for the printing of certain government publications.
The minister stressed that these were interim measures and that a permanent committee on publishing would be set up to prepare long-term policies. Still to be determined is the definition of a Canadian book and a Canadian publisher, but the minister is quoted in the Toronto Star, of February 12, 1972, as saying: "We definitely will help only Canadian houses". I just want to enter one caveat here. When the department is getting the list of Canadian books together, I hope we will not have a repetition, and I am sure we will not, of the selectivity that was forced upon the United States State Department in the infamous days of Senator Joseph McCarthy when people poked around to make sure that the titles were fit for the people to read. I think it might be extreme to expect the government to have Walter Stewart's book "Shrug" on all the book shelves, but if it does not have this type of book then there could be the danger that people would think there was censorship in the way titles were picked.
My first comment must be that these steps are very modest compared to the proposals submitted to cabinet last February, when the Secretary of State called for "immediate government action" before "the last resistance to the foreign flood collapses." In that memorandum the following recommendations were made: creation of a Canadian publishing development corporation; approval of the sum of $250,000 and two man-years for the activities of International Book Year; approval of the additional sum of $300,000 for the Canada Council for doubling its program of assistance in the area of creative writing and periodicals and study of additional measures.
The Secretary of State has made no special announcement regarding federal plans for International Book Year. His second cabinet proposal of September, 1971- these things keep pouring out-was for spending $450,000, not $250,000 on such programs as reading tours for Canadian poets and writers, book caravans to rural com-
Speech from the Throne
munities, French literature bookmobiles to Francophone communities outside Quebec, library programs, two special literary prizes, a special children's book prize, translation of important books and donations of paper and bookmobiles to underdeveloped countries. These are imaginative and valuable projects and it would be unfortunate if the government has decided not to pursue them.
Now I am going to skip a paragraph of my speech because my time is running out. While welcoming the program, most Canadian publishers agreed that it will only be of marginal importance. There is a clear need for additional measures. If we designate broadcasting as being vital to the development of national identity, invest large sums of public money in it and regulate both content and financial control, how can we neglect book publishing which is also important for the development of national ideas, values and identity?
I suggest some measures beyond the Secretary of State's proposals to be considered, as follows: first, federal-provincial discussions to develop a policy of institutional purchasing-libraries and schools-from Canadian wholesalers or publishers whenever possible. An estimate is that institutional purchasing outside the country for 1969 amounted to $40 million. Second, investigation of the distribution arrangements under the Combines Investigation Act; consideration should be given to a Canadian content quota system for paperback and magazine distribution racks. Third, the modernization and standardization of the tariff regulations to eliminate the bewildering array of separate items. Fourth, government encouragement for co-operation within the publishing industry for the compiling of basic data and also for standardization within the industry. Fifth, because children's books are so important as socializing forces, steps should be taken to encourage development of Canadian titles. In the centennial year there were prizes for children's books. Sixth and last, use of the CBC networks to draw more attention to the enjoyment and enrichment found in books.
Mr. Speaker, I have tried to give the House some ideas which, if they could be acted upon by this government, would aid our common purpose which is the purpose enunciated at the beginning of my speech, the promotion of the free flow of ideas by word and by image.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Speech from the Throne commits us to attack and overcome social inequality and isolation of the individual whether it be caused by lack of economic opportunity or remoteness from a mainstream of life. I agree with these proposals and express confidence that we shall go a long way toward our goal. There is another protection of individuals, however, the protection of all individuals in Canada, which I believe to be of overpowering urgency. It is protection of the public against unreasonable price demands and unreasonable wage and salary demands which bring about disruption and loss from strikes or the "rejection syndrome" under which a settlement which has been worked out by union representatives is later disavowed, with further negotiations, disruption and loss. Parliament and the legislative assemblies of Canada either alone or,

February 24, 1972
Speech from the Throne
preferably, with the co-operation of labour, simply must create the machinery whereby the public can try to protect itself from this immense and disturbing force.
For centuries, big business was the robber baron which had to be attacked, weakened and controlled. Today it is the large, organized unions which can wreak havoc on the whole public which is defenceless to defend itself. Big business has been controlled to a large extent by tough corporate laws and by anti-price fixing and anti- combines legislation. But organized labour has a special and privileged position in law. It has special status. Unions are not responsible for their illegal strikes or slowdowns, either to their employer or to others when they bring injury through loss of business or loss of employment. If the technicians who maintain flying equipment had to face the fact that they were responsible in law for any breach of the act, I am confident they would be there, they would be maintaining the machines and the aircraft would be flying.
I am not speaking for big business although some parts of it, particularly the pulp and paper and chemical industries, are in trouble. It faces tough international competition. I speak for the public, a large part of which is hurt every time there is a demand for an unreasonable wage or price increase. Just as the managers of big business used to think only of themselves and obtain the highest prices they could get while disregarding the public interest, so today many labour bosses are concerned only with what they can get for their own group; they disregard what is happening to the public. I ask, why are governments so reluctant to pass legislation which would allow the public to protect itself? I sense a change coming, and I hope it will come shortly.
I suggest that labour itself wants controls and that only relatively few of its political leaders wish to hold on to the power and notoriety of the strike. The vast majority of us, perhaps 75 per cent, are labourers in the sense that we are workers: this includes housewives, typists, farmers, technicians and all others who are not in management. All these people I have mentioned look to us, the Liberal party which makes up this government, to protect them. I believe the majority now feels that all strikes must be outlawed and a new system of settling disputes introduced, a system which would include protection for them, the public.
If the bakers can strike and force the retail price of bread to double, does the public not have an interest? Is it right that an organized union can bring about a price increase which can be passed on to the public without there being an opportunity for the public to object and be heard? If a crane operator, through his union, can force the construction industry to pay him $20,000 a year for a 40-hour week, is it not reasonable for the farmer to demand the same, or perhaps more, considering his investment? If the farmer were to do that, I submit the price of milk would go to $5 a quart. Of course the public is interested.
In Great Britain, one group caused personal inconvenience, physical discomfort and economic loss to everybody on the island. A few radar technicians in Canada who rejected the settlement worked out by their union

representatives have caused annoyance and interefered with our right to go about our affairs. They have endangered the lives, to some extent, of many and caused financial loss, directly or indirectly, to almost every person in Canada. This strike, following as it does a strike by the controllers, is hurting Canada far out of proportion to the number of people involved in the conflict. This just does not make sense.
In the United States a new group under the name Common Cause has organized to blunt the force of organized power groups which seek to and would take more than their share of the national income at the expense of others. There is mounting public concern for the elimination of costly strikes which can disrupt the welfare of a whole city, be they in private industry or in the public service.
Our strike record in Canada is notorious. I believe it is the worst, or highest of the world's leading industrialized nations. As a result, our prices have been increasing at about 4 per cent, and wage settlements at something over 7 per cent annually. This is far in excess of any increase in productivity and, of course, causes inflation. Inflation not only results from wage-price increase; it also comes about from disruption in the industry struck and in other complementary or service industries serving the struck industry. When union workers not on strike refuse to cross the picket line at a striking plant no matter what the cause, their refusal permits the striking union to spread its quarrel, and thus its injuries in the form of unemployment, inefficiency and inflation, far beyond its own reasonable jurisdiction.
If prices increase too much, the public can switch its taste and buy something else, or we can lower customs barriers. The public can do quite a bit to resist unreasonable prices. However, when it comes to wage and price demands, the employer is forced to settle at an ever increasing rate of increase and pass the increase on to the public which is defenceless. The public includes not only other organized labour but people who are not organized and are without any power to obtain a similar increase or any increase to offset the increased prices they must pay.
If, as I said earlier, a crane operator can force the construction industry to pay him $20,000 a year, why should not the radar technician demand a similar return? Why should not the industrialized farmer demand it? Considering the hours he works and the capital he has invested, he might demand such a return. I suggest that if the farmer were given the same rate of return as the crane operator or others in the construction industry, food would cost five to ten times as much as it now costs. Therefore I say the public interest has to be protected.
If inflation continues at between 5 per cent and 7 per cent, what will happen to capital and the ability to create jobs? The plant manager who budgets to save $100,000 in ten years, and utilizes his borrowing capacity to borrow $1 million in order to build a new wing for his plant and create 200 additional jobs, will find in ten years that the buying power of his savings will have shrunk to the buying power of today's $40,000 and he will not be able to do as he planned. If he waits another ten years, the buying power of his savings will be even more depleted.
February 24, 1972

The man with a fixed income has savings perhaps of between $25,000 and $50,000. He is a small capitalist. In ten years, with today's rate of inflation prevailing, the buying power of his capital will be cut in half. If a large capitalist has, say, $10 million, the amount required to create a large plant and create 500 jobs, he will find he cannot. In todays international market one must rationalize or specialize. To build a plant of half the size won't do. It would not be able to compete. Eventually, only the state will have the necessary funds and the capacity to own and operate big business. We will then have arrived at a state of complete socialism.
Just think where we are heading. We are heading for the situation which exists in the communist-socialist nations. In Yugoslavia and even Bulgaria a man can own his own home, a plot of land, the tools with which to work it, and a small business. The government, of course, owns and operates all big business. The government will allow an outsider to bring in $5 million and invest it and split the profit. He can take away 50 per cent of it.
Are we not, through inflation and our own greed, rapidly reaching the same place? This is the biggest threat in Canada today. With the drop in money value, millions are unable to live on their incomes, many more are unable to save for an emergency. More still will year by year see their savings depleted; they will be forced into a near-poverty position in circumstances which require government aid. This, in turn, will increase taxation generally and require yet more money from the private sector, making development even more difficult. No matter how wellmeaning the government might be, it can never keep up.
If we set out to ensure that every person in Canada received the same proportionate increase in income as the big, powerful unions can enforce, inflation would be far above 10 per cent a year. Inflation is a real threat to our society and, since it causes greater individual economic isolation and greater imbalance as between one area and another, it is a threat to the nation itself. I suggest:
1.	That all strikes be made illegal and an offence unless approved by the public as represented by a group of about 40 citizens impartially chosen from the province in question. They would act as a jury now acts to determine rights in both civil and criminal disputes, and as the United Nations seeks to act when two nations are in dispute.
2.	That all wages increases above a set amount, perhaps 2 per cent, be illegal and an offence unless approved by a similar jury.
3.	That Parliament give a clear direction that unions must assume full responsibility for their actions, as all other persons and organizations in society must do, many of them with less power and less capacity to affect adversely the public interest, by according them the capacity of suing and being sued and making them financially responsible for all damage caused by illegal acts, not only to the employer but to the public.
4.	That all unreasonable price increases-and this would have to be established after labour had become a fixed expense-be subject to turnback and penalty or a special tax. I am aware that if wages and salaries are controlled,
Speech from the Throne
we cannot leave a slack which somebody else might take up. Prices would have to be legally controlled as well.
Canada is now somewhat alone in the world with respect to trade patterns. All our governments are totally committed to promoting international trade by searching out new markets and urging greater productivity in order to lower production costs. We are in competition with nations such as Japan, whose people are united by group spirit which makes them a tightly-knit family devoted to production at a price acceptable in the international market.
We simply cannot afford the industrial conflict and the inflation which it produces to disadvantage us in world markets. To organized labour I say: I am not speaking against you. I am speaking, I believe, for the vast majority of you, for your wives, for unorganized labour and for all who must live on fixed incomes and who wish to see our economy on a sound, fair and healthy basis and moving forward for the good of us all.
Some will say that the restrictions I propose should be applied to those in essential public service only, at least at first. I find this point of view difficult to accept. Although the two air strikes have harmed the businesses of many people and denied employment to others, with resulting hardship, particularly in Mississauga in my constituency,
I am sure that a strike by International Nickel at Sudbury or General Motors in Oshawa would harm just about as many just about as much.
George Meany, who heads the AFL-CIO, said recently that strikes no longer made sense and should be done away with because they are causing increasing chaos and hardship to more and more people, and that strikes by people earning $7,000 a year or more no longer made sense. To them the strike is a double-edged sword. It is good to hear responsible labour speaking out in this way. I expect Mr. Meany's research department turned up the fact that though a member of a union might gain $1,000 a year, much, if not all of this advantage, was cancelled out if one took into account the other side of the ledger-the wages lost while on strike and the increased costs incurred for various products because of other strikes.
Mr. Donald MacDonald, president of the Canadian Labour Congress, when speaking to the Empire Club in Toronto in November, 1968, about stoppages, strikes and lockouts, said:
This is a price which we have to pay for preservation of the democratic process of collective bargaining and it is a price we are going to have to continue to pay unless and until somebody evolves a better method of settling disputes.
To Mr. MacDonald and members of the NDP I say: Would you be so committed to the use of force if unions were legally responsible for the results of their actions? Mr. Meany suggested binding arbitration. Is my suggestion so different? Workers demanding increases would go before a group of citizens not knowing whether they would be allowed as much as had been offered, or less. In most cases they would settle, knowing they would be dealt with by authority other than straight force.
Some will say it cannot be done, but if our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) can meet with Mr. Kosygin, and if Mr. Nixon can meet with the leaders of China and thaw the ice at least, surely our labour leaders can meet with gov-

February 24, 1972
Speech from the Throne
ernment and representatives of industry and work out a formula that would be worth a trial. If we were to succeed, we would make our nation the healthiest industrial nation in the world and the change would be for the benefit of all Canadians. If Canadian organized labour does not agree with my suggestion, I hope it will at least look seriously at the advice of Mr. George Meany and resolve to try to find a way of settling disputes which is more civilized, more just than the continued use of the strike and one which will not harm so many innocent people.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are told in the Speech from the Throne that it is the intention of the government that many areas of Canada be preserved in their natural state for the enjoyment of this generation and generations to come. Some of the grandeur as well as the wilderness of Canada's north will be guaranteed perpetual preservation through the creation of three large national parks north of the sixtieth parallel. The speech states further that these three parks, plus the seven new parks created since 1968, mean that for the first time in our history every province and territory will include within it a national park for the benefit of our people.
These are worthy ambitions and accomplishments. However, I wish to take issue with the government; they have shown lack of foresight and indifference to park development in my constituency, where an ideal opportunity exists for them to demonstrate to our people the sincerity of their policy to provide recreation areas where people can enjoy them.
The federal government is the sole owner of 17,500 acres in Grey county known as the Meaford tank range which has been declared surplus, and no area could be more ideal than this for park development. The Department of National Defence took over the tank range property on July 24, 1942. The farmers living there were required to vacate over 100 farms. Four schools and two churches were closed. There were 258 acres of apple orchards embracing over 8,000 trees, along with a sizeable peach orchard on Mountain Lake, which were sacrificed.
These people were reluctant to leave their homes. Many of the families and their ancestors had lived there for over 100 years. Furthermore, the price they were forced to take for their property was insufficient to establish a similar operation in another area. There was no consideration given to sentimental values. These people showed considerable loyalty, viewing their sacrifice as essential to the war effort. The area at large suffered a severe loss in the closing off of such a productive farm area.
To this day there is evidence of much sentiment in respect of this property. I have received many letters from people inquiring how they might go about getting their property or that of their ancestors back into family hands. Through this correspondence it was brought to my attention that there was a family graveyard in the range. Burials took place there from 1851 to 1937. The fishing operations from Vail's Point were the means of livelihood for several families. Mountain Lake was a popular place for sport fishing and family picnics. This lake and surroundings is one of the most beautiful areas in Ontario.

The Meaford tank range consists of 17,500 acres. Of this, some 15,000 acres are within impact or danger areas of former artillery tank and anti-tank ranges. Apart from impact areas, there are parts of the range which are known to contain unexploded munitions which strayed from normal trajectory because the shell hit the ground and the ricochet altered the intended impact area. It is difficult to determine how many acres could have spent ricochet rounds on them; it might well be some 1,000 acres. This leaves approximately 1,000 acres which were used for field exercises during which blank ammunition and certain types of training grenades were used. It also includes the roads and building sites. The area used for field exercises is relatively clear. The areas which are being used and are comparatively safe are the beach at Vail's Point, the boat launching area at Mountain Lake and the immediate vicinity of the administrative camp area.
The Georgian Bay shoreline within the confines of the range is approximately 12 miles in length. There are approximately 28 miles of roads suitable for travel by automobile. Ten thousand acres of the range are wooded. Mountain Lake is approximately 1 j miles long and 350 yards wide. The perimeter of the range is 25 miles. In seeking information I put this question on the order paper:
Does the Department of National Defence have trained personnel qualified to decontaminate the tank range target areas?
The answer was yes. But, as usual, an effort was made to sidetrack the issue by the following statement:
However, the number is small and there would not be enough qualified personnel to deal with a range decontamination project of such magnitude as Meaford.
In my opinion these are the men who should be doing the visual clean-up while sufficient numbers are being trained to do a complete job. In answer to a question in respect to the water system and the buildings, it was stated these were maintained until September, 1970, but that since that time they have not been maintained. I was informed it would require approximately 10 miles of fence at a cost of $42,000 per mile, to enclose the area contaminated so that the part of the range remaining could be certified safe. Fencing the range, in my view, would be a waste of money unless there were a few acres of known concentrated contamination in need of precautionary measures until an over-all clean-up was completed.
I will not take the time here to list all the questions I asked and their answers because some of them have been made public. However, I do want to say that from March 17, 1970, about the time it was rumoured the range would be closed, until October 15, 1971, I asked 20 questions in the House of Commons in respect of the range and converting it to a national park, and since November 4, 1971,1 have had 19 questions answered on the order paper.
The government did work up some concern and agreed to meet a deputation from the Grey county council here in Ottawa at an office of the defence department. The deputation received a briefing in respect of the contamination of the range and it was evident the department was trying to dodge the issue. However, they did agree to give consideration to suggestions the Grey county representatives
February 24, 1972

might care to make at a future date. It really amounted to a polite brush-off.
The promotion of a park in Grey or Bruce county has been one of my ambitions ever since I entered politics. In fact, on one occasion, after making an appeal to the Pearson government for park development in the Bruce peninsula, a cabinet minister told me: "If the provincial government would make a suitable area available, the government would develop a national park".
We now find ourselves with an area made to order and owned by the federal government. It is apparent from the many representations that have been made in the press, on the radio and by mail to me and to the government that the development of the range into a national park would bring the most benefit to the greatest number of people since the southern Georgian Bay area has been designated as ideal for recreation and tourism.
We are continually made aware of the thousands who visit our established parks, not only Canadians but many from abroad. A park in Grey county would be of easy access to millions of people in southwestern Ontario and the neighbouring states in the United States. It would bring in enough revenue to normalize the economy of the area, which is suffering under present conditions.
As early as July, 1970, the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development stated that "its national and histories parks branch considers that the tank range property is related closely to the Georgian Bay Islands national park complex and has a number of desirable features in terms of park use". There is very little shoreline on any lake or waterfront in southern Ontario that is not lined with cottages, and a national park on the range would preserve a few miles of shoreline in its natural beauty. Vail's Point could be developed into an ideal boating and yacht basin, a much needed accommodation in Georgian Bay in these days when more and more yachts ply our waters.
Mountain Lake has a good stock of fish. The 10,000 acres of woods provide good cover and refuge for the deer population and, under present conditions, is a game sanctuary. Excess deer population migrates to other areas where hunting is permitted. It is also a bird sanctuary where birds are not exposed to the many chemicals used so freely these days and which may be responsible for the scarcity of some species, notably the bluebird. It could be a bird watcher's paradise.
There are good ski slopes which the army used for training their ski troops. The existing buildings and the water system would all fit into the scheme of a national park. Visitors could arrive at the park by plane because the flying field and runway are in fairly good shape and could be improved. The range has the potential for a first-class national park and it is conveniently available to the area of southwestern Ontario where we have the highest concentrated population in Canada. These are the taxpayers who are making much of the new development possible.
We have been told the range is highly contaminated and dangerous, yet deer hunting has been carried on annually for many years, not only by the militia but by civilians as
Speech from the Throne
well, and they have travelled over much of the area. Many people have trespassed on the range, several as recently as the hunting season last fall. The militia and their friends have fished on Mountain Lake for many years. Snowmobilers have travelled over miles of the range.
Children have trespassed on the range. In answer to a question on the order paper I was told that two boys trespassing on the range in 1951, found a thunderflash and took it home. They removed the powder from the thunderflash and put a match to it. Both boys were severely burned when the powder exploded. This is the only recorded accident after 25 years of excessive trespassing. Happily, both boys recovered. The time will surely come when the people of the country will demand a clean-up at the range and some government is going to see that the job is done.
Does this government think that the people of the day are going to reconcile themselves to living with the fact that the largest part of the range will be left with its contamination for five generations or more? According to the opinion of the defence department, this period of time will necessarily have to expire before any degree of safety can be assured. Or, Mr. Speaker, are we going to insist the whole area be cleaned up in the same way we are eradicating pollution from the rest of our environment? The range was contaminated by the militia during the training of troops who were required to preserve freedom for Canada. This was a worth-while and necessary function. Now, after declaring it of no further use militarily, the government should have no hesitation in cleaning it up and returning it to the civilian population.
The information on file in the defence department indicates that the locations of 684 unexploded shells are known and the locations of 90 unexploded shells are not known. Furthermore, many of the shells are confined to the Sucker creek gully and the Hogshead at the west end of Mountain Lake. I was privileged to travel to all parts of the range which were accessible by automobile, in the company of an army officer. During the tour he pointed out many shells in the target area lying on the ground and some partly buried. It was my understanding that when a shell or other explosive was fired but failed to explode, its location was marked on a map.
I maintain the task of cleaning up the range can be accomplished, and for much less than the $150 million the government has estimated. This is a convenient figure used to discourage or delay any action on a clean-up program. This observation was confirmed by officers who spent many years in the militia. The Department of National Defence has personnel who are experts at locating and disposing of unexploded munitions, and the flimsy excuse they use in answering my question on the matter cannot be justified. If more men are needed, it is only a matter of selecting men to take the necessary training.
It is certainly a fact that it will be a dangerous job, but personnel of our militia are trained to protect our people in any emergency or existing national danger. The tank range contamination is no exception. The problem was created by the militia, and it is their responsibility to clean it up. At this point, I would like to quote from the Armed Forces Review, Ottawa Report on the White Paper on Defence:

February 24, 1972
Speech from the Throne
On the problem of getting the public to support a bigger defence budget the cabinet apparently senses that the public, in general, is apathetic about its armed forces and in order to justify an increased budget, the paper is trying to find something for the armed forces to do that is obviously peaceful and constructive.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the decontamination of the tank range surely qualifies as a peaceful and constructive project. In fact, it would be a challenge to the armed forces if they were given an opportunity to make it a reality. The government needs to display a little intestinal fortitude and get on with the job. In Grey county and surrounding counties there is practically unanimous agreement that the danger to humans on the tank range should be removed at the earliest possible date and action taken toward park development before the facilities there deteriorate any further. A Conservative government will not hesitate to enact the necessary measures to restore this beautiful area to the civilian population to whom it belongs.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I want to congratulate the mover and seconder of the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne, the hon. member for Bruce and Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Whicher and Mr. Lajoie).
The first, with his customary dynamism and eloquence, recalled the major achievements of the federal government, particularly in the field of social security, and mainly through fiscal relief, of the increase of old-age security pensions by the guaranteed income supplement, of the increase in pensions and allowances paid to veterans, etc. and our colleague, the new hon. member for Trois-Rivieres, also made a very outstanding maiden speech, which is to his credit.
Mr. Speaker, the Speech from the Throne dealt with the main issues of concern and interest to all Canadians at this time, such as the economy, industrial development, unemployment, exports, housing, agriculture, penal reforms, family income security, labour, the status of women within Canadian society, etc.
In order to cope with economic problems and support the expansion which has been making itself felt for some time already, to keep our competitive position on world markets, closer co-operation between government arid the business and industrial sectors is envisaged.
In my opinion, such co-operation is essential and is auspicious as the private sector will always supply most of the jobs and investments required for continued growth likely to give adequate impetus to all activities essential to the welfare and security of Canadians.
In a world where increasingly broader coalitions are being formed, often excluding us or at least placing us in an unfavourable position, and with a necessarily limited domestic market, we must absolutely aim for efficiency by putting science and technology to full use in order to assist such firms as are not afraid of innovating.
That task is one of the greatest challenges now facing Canada. That is what is called industrial strategy to be designed in keeping with characteristics peculiar to the Canadian economy and which will soon be announced, as the Hon. Minister of Commerce, Trade and Industry (Mr. Pepin) stated here yesterday.

Fortunately, Canada has numerous resources, the development of which surely spells progress; still, only orderly development, coupled with co-operation by private enterprise can ensure the evolution of our economy toward standards that better suit the needs of the future.
In the last few years, we have expected too much from our economy and we must avoid burdening it with expenditures that are unreasonable or rules that are too rigid in a country that is so vulnerable to foreign competition. Still, the co-operation must come not solely from the government but also from the representatives of industry and unions who must agree to avoid the turmoil of strikes which finally help no one and harm the Canadian people as a whole.
Forming industrial committees or councils in the various industries, groups composed of reputed experts from the three sectors who would study the various problems ahead of time, who would make recommendations on production, prices, wages, etc, strikes me as an excellent idea for we should all realize that an efficient formula must be found, before long; otherwise, we will eventually have to resign ourselves to controls-not voluntary at that-over prices, incomes, wages, with all the consequences that would entail, especially with regard to growth, investments and initiatives.
Thanks to intelligent planning, to our work and sacrifices, to discipline and common sense, through wiser use of our resources and co-operation, by remaining united instead of divided, we will surely give Canada the future it deserves, though there are now only twenty-odd million of us who live side by side with the greatest economic power in the world endowed with a domestic market of over 200 million people.
Mr. Speaker, to replace the now outdated and somewhat discredited Combines Investigation Act, the Speech from the Throne did announce the introduction of a newly revised and improved Competition Act along the lines of a bill which passed first reading during the session which ended a few days ago. This is to get to know the views of all those concerned in accordance with the participatory policy of this government-and indeed many representations have been and still are being received.
The purpose of this new legislation will be to protect consumers against truly harmful commercial practices without, however, inhibiting business operations, considering that agreements between individual companies are often useful and may even become a necessity.
Serious reservations have been made with respect to the proposed legislation, especially in connection with the duties and powers of the court which is contemplated and with the suggested procedure. The forthcoming consultations, as well as the consideration and discussion in this House and before the committee, should enable us to pass this legislation so vital in a field which is so important to the Canadian economy.
Mr. Speaker, a few months ago all the free countries of the world were faced with an economic crisis which for several of them was followed by radical changes but due to the foresight and shrewdness of this government our country has gone through this difficult period with far
February 24, 1972

fewer problems than most other industrialized nations. And according to the latest forecasts by international economic experts from the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development, the prospects in Canada for 1972 are excellent. An increase in the actual Gross National Product is expected, and it is believed that our country-and that without any mandatory control-has maintained the lowest rate of inflation among all member countries of that international organization.
Since we now have the highest ratio of labour as compared to the population, and in view of the ever rising participation rate mainly as a result of greater and greater numbers of women entering the labour market, the rate of unemployment has reached an alarming level despite increased economic activity. That will remain the constant concern of the government, as is mentioned in the Speech from the Throne. It must be noted however that more Canadians than ever before are working and that over 200,000 jobs were created during the year.
Besides, the most recent figures released a few days ago show that 25,000 jobs have been created in January 1972, and that over the past four months only the number of jobs has increased at an annual rate of 5 per cent, which represents an unprecedented rate of increase for this time of the year.
The various machineries introduced by this government ought to further decrease the rate of unemployment, when the effects of the subsidies of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, in aid to industry, make themselves increasingly felt and also when thousands of jobs are provided this winter through the excellent Local Initiatives program.

Speech from the Throne
