speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just before recess, I had time to speak briefly of various matters mentioned in the Speech from the Throne, such as our economy, future legislation on competition, the unemployment rate and the excellent results of the Local Initiative Programme in my constituency.
During the recent recess of Parliament, I met several small businessmen who informed me that assistance to existing industries was inadequate, that it is quite difficult to get a loan from the Industrial Development Bank or chartered banks under the Small Businesses Loans Act and that an agency should be set up to assist them in obtaining loans in special circumstances at more than reasonable rates, in order that they may overcome certain problems, finance profitable projects etc. I believe that

February 24, 1972
Speech from the Throne
suggestion deserves consideration by this government as additional assistance to industry.
However, the textile industry remains the main employer in my constituency, as in many other communities in Quebec and Ontario, and I have always taken an interest in this matter, like most of the hon. members concerned.
The textile industry is an extensive Canadian endeavour which provides 95,000 jobs in the primary sector, and more than 100,000 in the secondary sector. Fortunately, the government has realized that that industry, which had made constant efforts and large investments to improve its equipment and its techniques, and which can favourably compare with similar industries in other countries, except low-cost countries, needed a new orientation, and it implemented in May, 1970 a national textile policy which has so far had beneficial effects; some imports have decreased or are under greater control.
That industry needs a large labour force, and it is essential that it be protected, for I cannot fathom how it could be replaced, and its production and employment potential remains great.
Thanks to the efforts of the government and the industry the situation improved in 1971 as compared with 1970 and in the primary textile industry, for instance, employment increased by 3,725 between May 1970 and September 1971.
Forecasts for 1972 are optimistic provided consumption stays at its present level and the economic climate keeps improving. This is the opinion stated last month by the Canadian Textile Institute which admitted that the government's policy had encouraged industry, restored its confidence and stimulated investment. But improvements are still required since industry accounts for slightly more than half the total market of textile products and, per capita, we are importing much more than the United States, Great Britain and the European Community and this is an abnormal situation.
Lately, I was surprised to find that our trade balance with Japan was more or less on a par and even unfavourable this year, a situation which I think uncceptable while we are exporting almost exclusively raw materials required by that country and importing manufactured products such as textiles, electronic components, etc, which we could mostly produce here.
But there are other countries. I found yesterday while studying the latest statistics published by the Montreal Gazette that with Hong Kong and Taiwan our situation is even worse and, in one case, it was mentioned that last year we had been importing for over $80 million while exporting a bare $12 million. As other countries, it is high time that we take positive and efficient steps to protect our interests by setting in advance an acceptable level of importation and that we have an overall control policy regulating our import? from low-cost countries instead of relying on individual countries' action, a system which never worked.
Finally, our textile products policy should be announced in advance and for a rather long period of time so that this industry may plan its projects and investments.
Mr. Speaker, agriculture also involves a good many people in my riding, especially the dairy industry, and the dairy products price support plan has had beneficial effects and has brought about increased stability in our dairy farms. The producers I had the pleasure to meet recently seemed satisfied with recent improvements. The higher grants and larger quotas, the ordely marketing, the co-operation between producers, are all factors which helped increase the returns from industrial milk production. The average income which was $4.64 per hundredweight in 1967 is now up to $5.40; all the surplus milk that glutted the dairy market has now disappeared and the average production has greatly increased.
There still remains the problem concerning feed grain and its prices. This is a complex problem as I have seen it after meeting with representatives from the Catholic Farmers Union, etc.
The right hon. Prime Minister (M. Trudeau) in a speech he delivered to the Federated Co-operative in Montreal last February 2nd discussed the subject at length. He suggested possible solutions and I hope the equalization formula that was put forward will finally prevail.
The small farm development program announced in December will give the small farmers who want to remain as such the opportunity of building up profitable operations. The federal policy favours the family unit which is the best form of farming.
The national marketing Act will allow producers in several branches of agriculture, if they so desire, to work together and plan and organize the marketing of their products.
Mr. Speaker, the Speech from the Throne announced that the government pledges participation in legal aid. I trust steps will be taken to ensure that the provinces can extend the legal assistance that is already available, although almost exclusively in the larger centres and to a limited number of citizens, precisely because of limited means.
Mr. Speaker, although no mention is made of it in the Speech from the Throne, I expect the government will soon introduce a new bill concerning bankruptcies and insolvency, so that a more coherent and complete system can be set up that is better suited to the needs of our times. The Bankruptcy Act was last amended in 1966; since then, improvements were made in the managing of bankruptcies, but too many of them are still questionable or insufficiently controlled.
A study committee under the chairmanship of Mr. Roger Tasse tabled a report several months ago and made quite relevant suggestions. To my mind, the matter of introducing a new bill is pressing so that it can be studied and discussed as soon as possible by all interested parties.
Mr. Speaker, the Speech from the Throne announced several other interesting proposals which I shall not have time to discuss this evening. I am referring to the continued development of our national resources and the Canadian north, the promotion of more imports although these have already reached a record level, especially thanks to the participation, work and comptence of the Minister of Industry Trade and Commerce and his officials, which have earned him the admiration and respect of all Canadian industrialists.

February 24, 1972

The Speech from the Throne announces an elaborate, ambitous, exacting program which at times calls for long term solutions; still, they are appropriate under the circumstances, they meet the present needs of the country and its citizens and this program, Mr. Speaker, will get the support of all Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, before concluding my comments I would like to deal with a major problem affecting the constituencies of Brome-Missisquoi and Saint-Jean, that is the spring floods along the Richelieu River which especially those last years have caused considerable damage to the riverside residents and to all farmers whose lands are bordering the river and its tributaries in an area particularly suitable to farming. They have caused millions of dollars of damage and I realize that it is a complex problem as it concerns mostly the provincial government and the federal government to some extent and on account of the effect of these floods on the level of Lake Champlain the American authorities. I hope that the steps taken by my hon. colleague from Saint-Jean (Mr. Smith) and myself in co-operation with all the private agencies of the area will prompt the authorities to settle that problem as soon as possible.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like at the outset to congratulate the hon. member for Bruce (Mr. Whicher), the mover of the Address in reply, and the seconder, the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Lajoie).
As usual, the hon. member for Bruce has made a rather remarkable speech. As for the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres, he has shown in a brillant fashion that he is deeply interested in his constituents.
With many others I recognize that the Speech from the Throne has set some great objectives.
There is talk of increasing the national wealth through the development of a global industrial strategy and a more judicious use of science and technology, of asserting Canadian identity and protecting the environment, of developing and improving the quality of life for Canadians through better social laws and an improved legal system.
Such are the great objectives which this government has proposed to the Canadian peolein the Speech from the Throne.
I should like to take this opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to make a few remarks. I shall perhaps be severe occasionally but I should like to be most fair and pragmatic.
Considering the results for the past four years, surely I will not merely say that this government has not done anything. Surely, there have been efforts. We have and also certain difficulties, disappointments and achievements. Obviously, we cannot absolve this government so easily, considering that in 1968, this country had 300,000 unemployed and that today, this figure has swelled to 650,000.
On the other hand, I must admit that efforts have been made, at times in the field of textile products, at times in that of tax reform, which had long been needed. In agriculture some greatly appreciated changes took place and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Speech from the Throne
Pepin) has adopted a very sensible policy with regard to exports.
I have always been fascinated by the policy of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion which, taking into account the subsidies paid to Quebec, my own province, has given special consideration to regional problems. There again, the Local Initiatives program is a good policy. Unfortunately, it is too much of a short-term one which nevertheless has resulted in the creation of some jobs.
One must not forget either Bill C-262 with regard to the $80 million provided to fight the American surtax, with success, I believe.
Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, we must admit that those measures were appropriate and that an effort has been made. Did the results prove adequate? Did those efforts restore in Canada that economic stability which all of us are longing for?
Of course, there are two types of major problems: economic and constitutional and I should like to deal with them briefly. Indeed, I am convinced no hon. member would condemn a policy of full employment. But it seems to me that none of us has found the magic solution that would all at once bring about a policy of full employment.
We all agree to such a policy just as much as we agreed to the setting up of a just society. Nevertheless, it seems to me that with a little objectivity and co-operation we could get closer to this just society.
As far as stabilizing the economy of Canada is concerned, I had the privilege from time to time to recommend to the government many meetings with businessmen. Tonight I read in a newspaper that more than 1,000 Canadian businessmen will convene in Ottawa in March and April to meet Canada's High Commissioners for Trade. These conferences will be preparatory to meetings with the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, at which a solution to the slump in business will be considered.
It would certainly be important also to meet with the leaders of labour and employer organizations. I suggest that the government would have everything to gain by meeting these industrialists and businessmen more often than he has done to date. I have had the opportunity to ask that a summit conference be held on the subject and I do realize with great pleasure that efforts are made in that area.
It is obvious that no solution is forthcoming from this government. It is also obvious that opposition members or opposition parties have not found any solution either.
I believe the only way to create an appropriate economic climate would be to have the Canadian people participate in the decisions that must be made, by telling them about the difficulties the government is going through at the present time.
There is no shame in recognizing one's own inability to find a solution which has not yet been found. Should I ask the government to recognize their inability to bring forward such a solution, it might cause laughter among some hon. members, but I am sure that admitting one's own inability in finding the necessary solution in front of the Canadian people would be a proof of courage and honesty.

February 24, 1972
Speech from the Throne
It seems to me we have reached the point where the government really needs the advice of experienced businessmen and I believe that the solution probably lies there. A better informed public would show much more understanding and I believe that members of any party in the House could be invited to cooperate with the government more than we have up to now, all for the common good.
We have been looking for all kinds of solutions; short term solutions were devised. I had the opportunity and the privilege to offer and suggest some measures to the government. Tonight, I should like to ask the government to pay more serious attention to old age security and to availability of benefits at the age of 60. I know that the Speech from the Throne mentions social security measures. However, no details were provided as to whether the government intends to introduce a bill allowing people 60 years old to go into well-deserved retirement and receive, of course, an income exceeding by far that which is granted today. Considering that 300,000 or 400,000 people are aged 60 to 65, such a measure would greatly decrease the rate of unemployment and, at the same time, bring closer at hand a favourable social climate, because it is the government's responsibility to grant holidays to those who deserve them and to provide jobs for those in the working age group.
I should also like to call the attention of the government to the withdrawal of the 11 per cent tax which has repeatedly been mentioned in the House. I believe that it is the responsibility of each member of this House to remind the government that this measure apparently concerns each sector of the building industry; therefore, the government should approach those sectors directly or indirectly associated with construction and, with their co-operation, try to provide a credit large enough to bring about an increase in the number of housing units in Canada, subject, of course, to certain conditions. I still believe that the removal of this 11 per cent tax would result in new housing starts.
Mr. Speaker, I had an opportunity to read carefully some of the proposals pertaining to recreation which the responsible minister, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro), had in mind in connection with his future policy.
I noted today that the Minister of National Health and Welfare announced a $222,000 grant for four hockey programs in Canada which will be carried out during the winter. I think this is a timely grant and a very desirable policy. However, I would like to draw the attention of the Minister on the possibility of allocating certain monies to the construction of covered skating rinks or arenas in various municipalities in each province.
Having been active in sports circles for many years, I am sure several municipalities would be much interested in the building of skating rinks that would not necessarily be equipped with artificial ice as it is very costly. Nevertheless, I believe projects from $75,000 to $100,000 would be possible in thousands of Canadian municipalities.
The minister responsible for that should consider the possibility of establishing credit, 50 per cent of which would be provided by the federal government. It could be

discussed with the provinces. They could assume 25 per cent of the expenditures and I am sure the municipalities would be willing to pay 25 per cent. I think such a policy would create employment. Materials would have to be used to a certain extent and the project would enable hundreds of thousands of young hockey players to practice their favourite sport and it would enable Canada to train young people and keep them busy playing hockey.
I again emphasize the need for filtering plants in municipalities anxious to fight pollution. Indeed, it will always be in order to consider the possibility of issuing credits for such purposes and I always believe it would be good policy.
I said a while ago that agricultural measures had been passed these last years. I am referring in particular to Bill C-176 which is an indispensable tool to ensure the marketing of farm products and which was, I believe, one of the most useful legislative measures passed in this House during the last four years.
I should like just the same, Mr. Speaker, to say that Bill C-176 is but a tool, that its value will depend upon what the people responsible for its implementation will do. If we consider our experience with the feed grain policy in force for many years, I believe that Bill C-176 will be just as important.
No doubt, the government will soon change this policy so that eastern producers can enjoy the same benefits as their western counterparts, if we really want to have fair competition.
Bill C-176 will not be very effective unless the feed grain policy is changed. I appeal here to all eastern members, who I think know the problems of farmers, and especially of producers without an income who have been faced with this problem for a number of years and who consider this policy as discriminating against the producers of one area of Canada.
I do not think that eastern members have ever hesitated to approve grants to assist western producers, and I think our duty as eastern members is to ask our colleagues from the West to support our demands for changes which will be equitable for all producers.
I would also like to bring to the attention of this House the necessity for the government to seriously consider creating the new department which I had requested. I have already asked a question of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on this matter. He told me, without leaving me much hope, that a new minister of state attached to the Department of Agriculture would be appointed to represent eastern Canada.
In view of the complex problems of agriculture, I think it would be most advisable for eastern Canada to have a representative in the cabinet who would be in a position to discuss subventions. Moreover, if a minister of agriculture for eastern Canada was appointed, I think western Canada would also be entitled to have a minister of state who would be their official representative in the cabinet for agricultural problems.
In view of the existing complex problems, I think that all Canadian producers would welcome such an appointment.
I noticed in the Speech from the Throne that the government intended to introduce legislation regulating cigarette
February 24, 1972

advertising. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that the government will tackle to a greater extent the problem of educating the young or the public at large on the dangers of cigarettes, but I would expect above all that it will not limit itself to harassing the sectors directly related to tobacco. Having received many recommendations from my constituency and realizing that nearly all producers of cigarette tobacco in Quebec are in my riding, I often had the opportunity of talking with them. I know that the bill introduced last fall has caused them great concern, and I always wondered why the minister had not first taken the initiative of meeting the Canadian cigarette manufacturers. In my opinion, that question could have been resolved without alarming the whole sector involved in the production of cigarettes in this country. I dare say that an education program along those lines, similar to that on alcohol, should be desirable. An education program on cigarette tobacco could be launched.
Knowing full well that the special or designated areas will be reviewed on June 30, I shall take advantage of this opportunity, of course, to talk about my riding which has had the advantage and privilege of being recognized as a designated area. I should therefore ask the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) to pay special attention to conserving that designation; I would even dare ask a more special designation that might entail even more interesting advantages. The minister, who gave a favourable reply two years ago by recognizing a designated area in my riding, will surely not hesitate, considering the present economic situation which is as difficult as elsewhere in Canada, to consider the importance of the request I make on behalf of my electors.
Mr. Speaker, I wanted to make those few remarks. In the time I have left, I shall say a few words about a problem which may perhaps affect Quebec more particularly, that is, the constitutional reform. As a member from Quebec, it is my duty to fight for the interest of that province like all the other Quebec members who work here. I recognize that all the members of other provinces first have that responsibility; to my mind, we can perform our duties only by looking after the interests of our area, before and above all else, because in any event Canada benefits from it.
After four years, I must deplore the fact that not much progress has been made with regard to the constitutional reform. Must I point out, for the guidance of the members from the other provinces, that it would be enough to study once again the briefs presented at the federal-provincial conferences in the last ten years by the two political parties in power in Quebec, to know exactly what Quebec wants, and on what conditions Quebec can keep on hoping to live within the present system. I am thinking about the changes that have taken place in the last several years. Today, not only Quebec, but other provinces also, talk about decentralization of power and, in my view, Quebec has submitted some briefs that are weighty enough to show that it is imperative that such a policy of decentralization be introduced.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that, in fact, it is up to the Quebecers here in the House to establish such a policy. I must deplore the fact, however, that after four years it has not yet come about. I felt optimistic at one time, because of the large number of Quebec members on the government
Speech from the Throne
side and in the cabinet, and I believed that, because of this, an agreement could be reached between Quebec and the federal government.
I must now deplore that as far as telecommunications, social policies and family allowances are concerned, there has been and there are still some misgivings. I must also deplore the fact that the positions of the Quebec Minister of Health concerning family allowances have not been immediately endorsed.
Apparently other problems have arisen in connection with the policy recently announced by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) on the repurchase of small farms.
I have every reason to believe that the role of a Quebec member is to support Quebec's demands. I am aware of the co-operation that existed during the 1970 elections in Quebec between the federal and provincial Liberals. I must say that I am quite disappointed to note the lack of support given to those demands by the Bourassa government. I do not say that Quebec has not received grants. During the past four years, I think that Quebec has never received so many grants under various well conceived and justified policies for Quebec. But I think that is not enough because it will take more than short-term grants to please Quebec.
It is also important for a Quebec member in the House to inform hon. members from other provinces. I recall that in April 1970 I took the liberty of saying 15 days before the provincial elections that on account of the federal government's procrastination 20 per cent of Quebecers would probably vote for Quebec's secession. Many hon. members and newsmen were amused, but on the day following the April 29 elections they admitted that my forecast had not been that far off. Try as hard as we can to hide the two-nations problem and the principle of the particular status or the legislation that is of particular interest to Quebec, I feel it is a step backward to refuse to face this problem and discuss it in this House.
I am hopeful that the report on the constitution will be presented soon, according to the answer the Prime Minister gave me this week in reply to a question I asked him. Once this report is tabled, I hope we will succeed in bringing about a debate on constitutional reform. I know an election is near at hand. Perhaps it is not quite fair to speak of constitutional reform at this time, but I feel it is my duty to inform hon. members that it is imperative for the future of Canada to seriously consider Quebec's demands and for every Quebec member to inform his colleagues from other provinces instead of trying to make them feel that those who believe in the independence of Quebec are few in number.
The figures are there and I believe constitutional changes might really prove to Quebecers that their future is still in Canada. We would thus have done something positive. These remarks are being made in that spirit, in order first of all to invite hon. members from other provinces to realize the situation prevailing in Quebec.
I recognize that certain provinces require special legislation as we realize that differences exist between provinces. I feel that Quebec also must succeeed in having its differences accepted and if we seriously accept such

February 24, 1972
Speech from the Throne
recognition we will be contributing to building a better Canada.
Allow me, Mr. Speaker, to call upon the federal government's special co-operation for the James Bay development project which has been discussed for several days in the House. I trust that those who made comments did so in a positive manner.
The James Bay development project is specific to Quebec. It will benefit the country as a whole. The federal government should also offer its co-operation by way of services, grants and loans in order that the government of Quebec may actually find the amounts required to carry out this project in Canada.
Before closing, I should like to mention that the Speech from the Throne makes no mention of a reform which is essential in this Parliament. It has to do with limitation of debates. I know the government attempted to introduce such an improvements. Once more I appeal to objective hon. members, asking them to give serious consideration to "limitation", "scheduling" of debates. There is a tendency to plan everything today, and I believe we have omitted to program ourselves. It would be well that hon. members seriously consider limiting debates in order to give Parliament greater efficiency. I do not feel we can continue to speak of efficiency in view of the time we have wasted since I have been in the House.
I sincerely hope, Mr. Speaker, since my time seems to have expired, that my remarks will get particular attention from those who are responsible for the policy to be worked out to correct some shortcomings that we have in this country. I am confident that my appeal, both to hon. members from Quebec and from other provinces, with respect to economic and constitutional problems will receive special attention from everyone and lastly that the Parliament of Canada, through serious and effective programming, will succeed in getting back the confidence of Canadians, through serious work that will give them satisfaction for the benefit of our country, Canada.

speechtext:
-and I am prepared to say, indeed I am prepared to assert, that it is a lot better to be an old person today than it was 25 years ago. But as a Liberal member said earlier today, that is not the point. The point is that we should be making of the later years of our existence what the poet Robert Browning had in mind when he said:
Grow old along with me!

The best is yet to be,
The last of life, for which the first was made.
I welcome as strongly and as warmly as I can all the things that are being done to meet the problems of our youth. I welcome the Opportunities for Youth program of last year and I am glad there is to be one this year. I think there are a great many things we must do to make life more hopeful, more promising, more exciting for the young people of this country. I should like to suggest that one of the ways that we can contribute to a better life for our younger people is to make it possible for many more of our older people to leave the labour market so there will be more jobs for those who are younger.
Let me make it clear that I am not asking just for an increase here or an increase there of a few dollars in one pension or another. I am not asking just for supplements on a means test or an income test basis. I am not asking just for pensions to be raised so people can maintain the level of existence they have had. I am asking for a massive effort to make old age one of the best and most exciting periods of life.
I suggest that one of the ways to do this, one which fits in with an acceptable, decent and civilized philosophy of life, is to accept the fact that there comes a time when people ought no longer to have to work to stay alive but, having made their contribution, they should have a sufficiently high guaranteed income to engage in pursuits that will make life interesting for them and that will contribute to the excitment and the interest of life as a whole. I am asking the members of this Parliament to get over the notion that when we talk about old age pensions all that is meant is welfare or supplements or sufficient dollars to keep body and soul together. I want us to talk about old age as a portion of life that should be made the best of all the years we are on this earth.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I think the time has come for this Parliament to look at all the pension plans that come under our jurisdiction; indeed, to look at the whole question of pensions in our society and not be satisfied with just a piddling increase here or there. The time has come to review and upgrade all our pension plans, making them programs that will produce the kind of life that I have suggested for all those of older years.
I intend from this point on to be specific and to make suggestions that I think should be accepted regarding the various pension plans that come under the jurisdiction of this Parliament. I refer, first of all, to the Old Age Security Act. I still think that when that act was first passed and came into effect on January 1, 1952, it was one of the most advanced pieces of social legislation ever passed in this country. That act still is, in its basic elements, an advanced piece of social legislation, but some of its virtue has been lost by the introduction of an income test into part of the pension paid under it.
I think the time has come for the pension payable under that act to be raised to $150 a month across the board, without any means test or income test in it at all. I also urge that the escalation of the pension be re-established for everyone. At the present time the escalation applies only to those people who get a guaranteed income supple-
February 24, 1972

ment on top of the $80. This means that those who get only the old age security pension have it fixed at the $80 level until Parliament decides otherwise.
I suggest that an escalation element should be restored to the entire pension and that it should not be an escalation limited to 2 per cent per year. When the cost of living is increasing by 4 per cent or 5 per cent per year, to raise the pension by only 2 per cent per year is to condemn the recipients of it to a losing battle. The least that should be done is that the pension should be increased each year by the full amount of the increase in the cost of living.
I go further than that. In these better years that I am talking about, our older people are entitled, not to only enough to keep up with the standard of living that they had when they went on pension, but to share in the increased standard of living. They are entitled to share in our increased gross national product. We should find an even better formula than the cost of living index for our pensions, bearing in mind that what we should be talking about is not pensions as a form of welfare, just so many dollars to keep a person's body and soul together until he dies, but we should be making that period of life one of the best in human existence.
Not only do I call for the old age security pension to be raised to $150 a month and for a proper and adequate escalation feature to be reinstated, but the time has come to write into the act a provision enabling anyone who meets the other qualification, namely, a certain length of residence in Canada, to draw the pension at age 60 provided he is prepared to leave the labour market or is out of the market, as is the case with many people, particularly spouses of pensioners.
This is a theme I shall repeat as I talk about some of the other pension programs that come under our jurisdiction. I have also heard it suggested tonight and during the course of this debate by others, in passing. I am making it the whole burden of my speech. The time has come, not just to retire a few people here and there so there can be a few jobs for 25-year olds, but to make a massive effort to make it possible for people age 60 or over to leave the labour market in order to pursue other things which would make life interesting for them and to create more jobs at the other end. It will not only create jobs for those of younger ages by virtue of the fact that if a person who is older leaves a job, somebody else can move into it. If one accepts the kind of program I am advocating, namely pensions that will enable all our people to live in decency and dignity in their retirement, it is going to cost something. In fact, I am surprised there has not been an interjection already asking from where the money is going to come.
If the kind of program I am advocating is put into effect, a lot more work will have to be done to produce the goods and services to enable the older people to live without working. It might even require the employment of about 650,000 people. I suggest that is something we need in Canada today, with that number now unemployed.
One of the ways to meet the objective stated by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) this afternoon, namely, that he does not want to see even one person unemployed in Canada, would be to accept the kind of program that makes it possible for people aged 60 and older to leave the
Speech from the Throne
labour market. Work will have to be done to provide for their needs. In this way jobs will be created for those of working age.
I move on to the Canada Pension Plan. Here, too, there should be some major amendments. One of them is a change such as I have been suggesting for the Old Age Security Act, namely, making it possible for persons who leave the labour market to draw their full Canada Pension Plan benefit at age 60. We already have that principle in the Canada Pension Plan. One already receives it automatically at age 70, but anyone can get it at age 65 if he leaves the labour market.

I suggest that principle be extended by permitting all those who leave the labour market at age 60 to draw their full Canada Pension Plan benefit at that time. I am trying to emphasize that with pensions of this kind, $150 a month old age security and full Canada Pension Plan benefit at age 60, there would be an inducement to many people in that age bracket to leave the labour market, let alone the fact it would solve the problem of those who are forced out of the labour market by today's economic conditions.
I also urge that the Canada Pension Plan be amended, as suggested by the Royal Commission on the Status of Women, to make it possible for married women who are at home to draw benefits in their own right under the Canada Pension Plan. There are various ways this can be done. Payments can be made by them or for them. The principle is one that I think is right. I commend the Royal Commission on the Status of Women for having proposed it. This is something we should do at the earliest possible moment.
If we were to make just these two sets of amendments I have talked about, amendments to the Old Age Security Act and the Canada Pension Plan, there would be enough pension money available at age 60 for thousands of our people, for thousands of married couples, to encourage them to retire. It would have a real effect on the employment situation as well as on the goods and services that would have to be produced. I suggest that on all counts it is an economic move that we would be foolish not to pursue without further delay.
In passing I should like to say a few words about one other pension plan that comes under our jurisdiction, one that we do not refer to very often. That is the pension for the blind. In the old days, the Old Age Security Act, the Old Age Assistance Act, the Blind Persons Act and the Disabled Persons Act were dealt with concurrently. If the pension under one was increased, it was done under the others. We have altered all that. The Old Age Security Act is on a different basis and the Canada Assistance Plan has taken over from some of the others. In the process, the pension under the Blind Persons Act has stayed where it was, at a basic $75 a month. The least we can do for our blind people is provide them with the kind of pension I have talked about. Like the old age security pension, the blind pension ought to be $150 a month. I urge that there be such an amendment to the Blind Persons Act.

speechtext:
With regard to retired public servants, I am still proud and a bit excited over the tremendous move we made a couple of years ago when we provided for the pensions of retired civil servants to be escalated every year if the cost of living went up during the previous year. The result was that many of our retired public servants got a pretty good boost a year or so ago and they receive an increase every January. But that increase is tied to a 2 per cent ceiling. When the cost of living increases 4, 5 or 6 per cent in a year, and these people only get a 2 per cent increase in their pensions, they are fighting a losing battle.
I plead that the same thing be done for them that I have argued for in respect of old age security, namely, that the least we do is increase those pensions by an amount which reflects the full increase in the cost of living. But in my view that is not enough. I want these people not only to get enough to buy the same basket of goods and services, but also to be able to share in the rising standard of living that a new generation is able to produce because the older generation brought it to that point.
So I urge this kind of improvement in respect of the Public Service Superannuation Act and in the acts which govern the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the Canadian armed forces and others. In passing I put in a word, as I do every couple of weeks, for the retired RCMP and armed forces personnel who are not yet 60 years of age but who are denied the increase they will get after age 60 because that was written into this special legislation a couple of years ago.
I have said several times that any argument the government had for this is gone. In the new arrangements made last year for public servants to retire at age 55 and some between 50 and 55, it was provided that they get the escalation in their pension then without having to wait until they are 60 years of age. Since this is now possible for public servants under 60 years of age, I think it is grossly unfair and is gross discrimination to deny this increase to RCMP and Canadian armed forces personnel who have not yet reached age 60.
There are quite a few other changes which need to be made in all these acts under our jurisdiction affecting employees of the ftderal government, but in the main the 
sort of thing that needs to be done is to provide for adequate escalation consonant with the increase in the cost of living and the increase in the standard of living.
May I also point out that there are changes having to do with the retirement age that could be made. The changes made last year were in part good in that at age 55 a public servant with 30 years' service can retire on the full pension he has to that point. I believe we should encourage the possibility of these people retiring, say, any time after age 50 on the full amount of whatever pension they have earned. Old age is not just a period of life when we come with a bit of charity or supplement to keep people alive; it is a period of life when we should be making the best of all our years on earth.
Now I come to something mentioned just a moment ago by my good friend across the way. He did not need to suggest it, for I have been speaking on this for 25 or 30 years. I refer to the pensions of CNR employees. Here, again, I want to express pleasure that at long last, about a year ago, one change was made and CNR pensioners who were then retired received an increase covering the years they had been retired. But there is one serious shortcoming in that. It was a one-shot proposition. Retired public servants get their 2 per cent increase every year as long as they live, but the CNR pensioners got it last year only. They do not get any further increase this year and there are no other increases in sight for them. I contend that this escalation of pensions of retired CNR employees should be put on an annual basis at least the same as is done in connection with retired public servants.
But, again, although I ask for these things and use the words at least, I am not satisfied with a 2 per cent ceiling, or an increase related only to the cost of living; but it would be a start to get that much. A year ago the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) said that anything further would have to be negotiated, but it seems to me the chances of that happening are not very bright and what is needed is for this government to make to Canadian National Railways the same kind of representation it made over the years for an initial escalation, only now the representation should be for an annual escalation in CNR pensions.
There should also be a complete review of the formula under which CNR pensions are calculated. I put it in the simplest terms. The employees are asking that their pensions be based on a 2 per cent factor, that is, that their pensions be calculated on the basis of 2 per cent for each year of service. That is the story with the public service; that is the story with many good pension plans. Our own is even better but I shall not talk about it tonight, for my views about our own plan are on the record. I believe that Canadian National Railways being a government-owned company, it is one which ought to pay some attention to views like this when they are expressed in Parliament. It is also an organization which ought to be told by the government what it should be doing in this field.
Let us not stop with making representations to Canadian National Railways. The Canadian Pacific Railway needs to have some pretty strong things said to it. At long last, after something had been done for retired public servants, for retired RCMP personnel, for retired armed services personnel, for Canadian National employees and a lot of other people, the CPR came through with some-
February 24, 1972

thing. But I wonder how many members of this House have examined that "something" to find out how little it is. In particular, I cannot speak too strongly of how iniquitous I think it was for the CPR to say that any of its employees who retired prior to January 1, 1956, were to get no increase whatsoever. That is still the case today. Many, of course, have died since the change was made and many more will die before anything can be done.
However, I believe a pension increase of that sort, made somewhat comparable with what was done for retired public servants, somewhat comparable with what was done for CNR employees but which left out all the old-timers who retired before January 1, 1956, was something of which even the CPR with its thick hide ought to be terribly ashamed.
Mr. Speaker, I see my time is going on. However, there is another piece of legislation which comes under our jurisdiction which I think we should also look at very thoroughly. That is the Pension Benefits Standards Act. This is a fairly new piece of legislation and I am glad it is on our books. We have it federally and at least four provinces, perhaps more by now, have similar legislation. These various acts are statutes which determine the conditions pensions under federal or provincial jurisdiction must meet. We have laid down in the Pension Benefits Standards Act some pretty important requirements that pension plans which come under federal jurisdiction have to meet in order to get registration and in order to qualify for income tax deductibility. So we do have a fair control over the pension plans of the railways, the airlines, the banks, the steamship companies and the elevator companies. All these employers come under federal labour jurisdiction.
To the extent that the provinces in their legislation tend to match what we put into the Pension Benefits Standards Act, we are in a strong position to determine what private pension plans ought to provide. I think one of the things we should write into the Pension Benefits Standards Act is the requirement that every pension must have in it a provision for escalation.
I assert, Sir, that the day of a fixed pension is for the birds. The day is gone when any human being no matter whom he worked for should be asked to go out on a pension and stay at that level for the rest of his life. I think we should say to the companies whose pensions are registered under own legislation-and I think the provinces should say it to those employers who come under theirs-that a pension is not a pension and a plan is not approved unless there is a provision in it for pensions, once started, to be escalated at least according to the increase in the cost of living. But again I say that I think it should be according to the increase in the standard of living. That is something which we should be writing into our Pension Benefits Standards Act.
Maybe I am looking somewhat ahead, but another point which should be written into that legislation is early retirement, which I have tried to stress through all my remarks tonight. I think that just as I want written into the Old Age Security Act and the Canada Pension Plan the provision that people can retire at 60 if they leave the labour market, so I think private pensions plans should
Speech from the Throne
have the same kind of provision in them. To me this is the point we have reached.
I came here in a day when we fought to improve pensions which were only $20 a month and we thought we had a victory when we got them increased to $25 or $30. In those days it was a case of keeping body and soul together. But times have changed. We are fast moving into an era where the work ethic is disappearing, an era in which people have rights because they are people, not because they have done a certain type of work. To carry out all that, I think we have the obligation, indeed the right, to fight for pensions across the board that include escalation after they are put in pay, and also for pension plans that include provisions for early retirement.
Before my time is finished I should like to say something about one other group of pensioners. I deliberately left them to the last because I think their case is particularly important. We control entirely, in the Parliament of Canada, the question of the pensions that we pay our veterans. I have had the privilege of being a member of the Veterans Affairs Committee, and last year we made certain improvements. I am pleased that they were made and I am glad to be able to say that many veterans are better off because of the changes that were made in the Pension Act and in certain other pieces of veterans legislation. But the fact that they are slightly better off is beside the point.
It is still urgent that the basic rates paid under the Pension Act-basic rates for disability pensions-should be increased, and it is also extremely urgent that the allowances that we pay under the War Veterans Allowance Act should be increased and that the means test provisions in that act should be greatly modified if not done away with altogether. I speak as one who believes strongly in the concept of the guaranteed annual income- not a means test supplement such as we get from the other side but a truly guaranteed income-that some day will be available to everybody. I believe it should start now for all our older people, and a particularly good place to start it would be with our veterans.
Just as I have suggested that old age security should be available at the age of 60 to those who are prepared to leave the labour market, I would do for veterans as we used to do in another context; I would lower that age for them. I would say that any veteran who has had war service-and he does not have to prove anything else- should, not later than at the age of 55, be able to get a sufficient pension to enable him to leave the labour market and to enjoy a little more of that exciting period in life that we call old age, because of the service that he gave to his country.
I make this plea both for veterans and for all our older people as strongly as I can. I am not standing up here asking for another 42 cents or for another $5 or $10. I am asking for a whole new approach, a new rationale, a new philosophy about old age. It must not be a time when we just keep people around until they are carried out to the cemetery; it is a time of life which should be made the very best.
It can be done, and I repeat that in doing it we will not only be making things better for our older people but we will be requiring a tremendous amount of work to be done

February 24, 1972
Speech from the Throne
to produce the necessary goods and services. Thus we shall be putting our younger people to work as well and helping to solve the pressing problem of mass unemployment. .
Therefore, I commend to the government and to this House the suggestion I made at the beginning of my remarks, namely, that we launch a massive effort to make things really better for the older people of this country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with this Throne Speech we are nearing the end of the four-year period of the present administration. First, I should like to add my congratulations to the mover and seconder: they did quite a good job on such a poor document.
Now I would like to examine the four-year record of this government. After the long years of minority government, the people of Canada were perhaps expecting and hoping for a majority government even though they might not have necessarily agreed with the party in power. The electorate were led to expect a good deal from the just society, but the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) was quite right when he said that the just society is only for the Grits. Now it does not seem to be for anyone, even for the Grits.
Let us look at what this administration has done for the country. I would like to agree with one thing that the hon. member who preceded me said in his speech with regard to the great consternation about freezing old age pensions at $80 a month. The old people, in the years when they were paying sales tax and income tax, were led to believe that a pension would be given them regardless of their station in life or their income. Now they find their pensions frozen and they are most unhappy about it.
When the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was elected he was expected to unite the country, or so people thought. There was to be an official languages bill to unite the two main language groups in Canada. The languages bill was to avenge the French for the Plains of Abraham and do justice to the English. What has happened? Canada is more disunited than ever. Quebec is under strong pressure to declare that province unilingual in order to safeguard what the Quebec people believe is a continuation of their language and culture. A severe backlash is developing in the rest of the country against this bilingual policy and we may well experience a severe confrontation in which surely no one will win.
We are at loggerheads with the United States, our neighbour to the south. The Prime Minister declared in Russia that the United States was a cultural, economic and even military threat to Canada. On his return to Canada, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) went scurrying south to carry the message that Canadians loved their great neighbour and invited Americans to invest their dollars in Canada.
We know that for western Canadians the period this government has been in office has been one of alienation and many western Canadians in their multicultural society are having second throughts regarding the value of confederation. The new tax structure will have a particularly severe impact on western Canada, with its strong bias against the resource industry and against the individual entrepreneur. In many ways the attitude this

government has adopted has meant a reversal of the days of the Northwest Fur Company, when the whole of the western lands were subservient to Montreal fur interests.
The period this government has been in office has been a trying time for the agricultural community in western Canada. Since 1968 we have witnessed a precipitous drop in the grains income of the whole of western Canada. The grains income in the years 1966-67 and 1967-68 amounted to $1,400 million and $1,300 million respectively. The year 1968-69 saw a drop in the income of the grain industry to around $850 million. Had any other community or any other segment of the Canadian economy experienced a one-third reduction in their gross income at a time of continually rising prices and rising costs of production, there would have been widespread outcry and disastrous results.
What did the government do? In the years 1968-69 the government sat supine while export markets all over the world were lost to Canadian grain. The survey of that year will show that we sold barely 150 million bushels of wheat, although the export figures would be slightly better due to shipping changes. It was a disastrous year for Canadian exports of wheat and barley. It can be said that there was an almost complete sales failure in the 1968-69 crop year. During the whole of the year the goven-ment did almost nothing to increase Canadian grain sales.
Through the Wheat Board, as the handling agent of western farmers, there was nothing that farmers as a group could do but exhort the government to use their influence to alleviate the situation. If anything, the 1968-69 crop year was a reminder that whatever the Wheat Board might be, it has to be an agency to sell grain. If, in the government's wisdom, farmers are to have an income supplement policy to increase their income, it is not to be done through the Wheat Board. The board's duty is to sell grain on the world market at a competitive price. The disastrous loss of sales in 1968 and 1969 are still being felt both in volume and in loss of income.
The following years have shown an increase in the movement of grain. But for the large failure of the American corn crop last year our marketing situation would have been much more serious. This year the grain industry seems to be running into further trouble. The warning of Mr. Vogel, head of the Wheat Board, that the world price of wheat has softened considerably brings no comfort to the western grain industry.
And what about the ill-fated stabilization bill, a bill that would have relieved the government, at least in the 1970s, of contributing any significant amount from the federal treasury to augment grain income? With the phasing-out of the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act and the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, $50 million to $60 million that the western farmers had received each year in the previous 15 years had to be replaced with a formula whereby there would be little or no chance of payout in the decade of the seventies. As well, the farmer would have had to subsidize the fund to the extent of 2 per cent of his gross earnings, so that his levy alone would have been almost certain to carry any payout under the plan in this decade. Small wonder, then, that the stabilization plan found little favour with the opposition and the farmers.
February 24, 1972

Now we have a two-price system for grain. But it is not really a two-price system at all. It is merely a formula for calculating an amount of money to be taken out of the federal treasury and paid to the grain producers of Canada. Suffice it to say that a suitable stabilization plan for income supplement has not been produced by this government.
Then there is the passage of Bill C-176. This is a bill designed to implement supply management. The market sharing arrangements can result only in the decrease of quotas, with the productivity in the prairie provinces to be transferred to the central provinces on a purely political basis. It is a far reaching bill. It obviously will take the livestock industry, eggs, chickens, turkeys, pigs and cattle and abrogate the market and implement drastic changes in the producing and selling aspects of the industry. Like the dairy industry, Bill C-176 is designed to transfer the meat industry from western Canada into the more central areas. This can only cause a more marked reduction in the production of meat in western Canada and have the effect of further reducing the ability of the agricultural community to sustain its population in western Canada.
With this exercise in supply management we are heading into a period of rigid controls within the whole agricultural industry-a type of control that can only make for inefficiencies, that can only make for increased cost to the consumers without any real increase eventually in the price to the producers. The establishment of quotas means the reduction of the agricultural population at a faster rate and further alienation of the western agricultural industry. It means that we have virtually removed ourselves from the possibility of export markets for our meat products. Bill C-176 will eventually result in demands that manufactured products be prevented from free movement within Canada.
I should like to quote from the Manitoba Co-operator of February 17, which says this about Bill C-176:
Surely this is a lesson that has been learned from the experience of the nations of the European Economic Community. Trying to dismantle the overbearing economic costs of agricultural production distortion is now the main preoccupation in Europe. And, at the same time the European farmer has not improved his individual lot one iota. He is economically depressed and unhappy. With the production potential of the United States adjacent to us on this North American continent there is even less hope of even limited temporary success in legislating parity to a deficient resource area.
And certainly western Canada with her whole economic future tied up in the welfare of the primary industry of agriculture cannot concede on this issue.
To those who do not come from agricultural ridings I would suggest that Bill C-176 will have considerable effect in the years to come.
This government is now involved in the problem of how to deal with our enormous neighbour to the south. With the strong nationalist feeling demonstrated in the anti-Americanism of the Prime Minister and his succinct statement that he found the United States a cultural economic and political threat to Canada, he arraigned himself on the side of those who found great comfort in baiting the American eagle.
We witnessed the Prime Minister's Washington journey. He returned saying he had won a great victory over the Americans. What is happening now? On one day we have
Speech from the Throne
the Prime Minister telling the House of Commons about the tough line the government is taking with the Americans and that it will continue to be tough; then we have the external affairs minister (Mr. Sharp) in Winnipeg saying Canada is prepared to make unspecified concessions to the United States to prevent a serious rift between the two countries because of disagreement over the automobile agreement.
So our relations with the Americans are now in limbo, but it is costly for us. We really cannot afford a policy of "wait and see". Until last August financial relationships between Canada and the United States were more or less clearly defined. As long as there is definition, each party knows where the other is and businessmen can act accordingly-but uncertainty is now the order of the day.
There is the American DISC legislation, an act of the American government that will have serious effect on our industry, an act that really the so-called Canada-firsters, the Committee for an Independent Canada, should wish to be passed because it will mean the repatriation of production now undertaken in Canada to be carried out in the United States. These people are peculiarly quiet at this stage. DISC will be a financial inducement for an American to export to Canada what is now being produced in Canada.
What are we doing? At a time when we are increasing our tax on industry by means of the recent tax changes, the Americans are making a better climate for their industry. There are many areas that need to be defined in our relationships with the United States. Take the decision of the National Energy Board to change in midstream the rules and the guidelines under which the export of natural gas would be allowed. It smacks very much of influence by the government, on a purely political basis, to prevent the export of natural gas on terms that were previously agreed upon. There is a feeling that the Americans need our natural resources in ever increasing quantities and that either we should not sell to them or we should sell them at a price that is much greater than we are presently receiving.
In dealing with the matter of foreign control we have shown great inconsistency. We have been since 1969 awaiting the Gray report on foreign ownership. The delays have been endless and we are still waiting. The policy of the government is purely ad hoc. They improvised in the sale of Home Oil and they improvised in the deal with Denison Mines. All the actions of the government indicate complete confusion.
What about the Canada-United States auto pact? Its value may well have been overestimated. Our exports and imports would both be lower, but in a truer perspective if we disregarded the auto pact figures. The auto pact is primarily an arrangement among the parents and subsidiaries of United States automobile manufacturing companies, sanctioned by government. It seems likely that with the attitude of American unions that more manufacturing be done at home, with the decision on where autos are to be produced being made in Detroit, the auto pact could be reduced in value and may eventually become meaningless.
So this administration is powerless to negotiate with the American administration, the Nixon administration, an

Speech from the Throne
administration that views the Canadian government with a deep-seated suspicion of having a love affair with its enemies. It seems likely that we will again have to deal with the Nixon administration after the November election, a prospect which this administration must view with considerable horror. The Manitoba Co-operator carries an article, reprinted from the Globe and Mail, which in part reads:
We have been kept in the dark for the good of two governments, not for our own good. In Canada, at least, we are probably in real jeopardy until those two elections are over.
The author of that article is referring to our election and that of the United States. I should like to say a few words about the Official Languages Act, Mr. Speaker. This act has caused severe dislocation in our civil service and has not in any way helped to correct the situation for which it was designed. It has failed because of a peculiarity of human nature. The fact is that no one is bilingual; a person has a mother tongue and a working knowledge of a second language. The present official languages legislation has worked to bring about the almost complete exclusion of the merit principle in the civil service. I think it has caused disruption in the civil service and will cause increasing tension in the future.
The administration of the act is open to all manner of bias, favouritism and discrimination, real or imagined. Of course, so far as the individual affected is concerned, real or imagined grievances are equally bad. Our having decided to adopt an official languages policy really means that everyone in Canada must by definition be a Francophone or an Anglophone in order for people to fit into the official languages category.

speechtext: Come on, now.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
This has not satisfied the province of Quebec and the French communities in that province are jealously protecting their language rights, rights which we all agree they ought to have. There is at present severe pressure on the provincial government of that province to declare French as the official language of the province. This necessarily means that English will become a secondary language, which indicates that the official languages policy in Ottawa has not, in the opinion of that province, met its needs.
Similarly, from the Anglophone point of view, the enunciation of the official languages policy has meant that effectively the unilingual Anglophone has been shut out of the decision-making process in the civil service as well as all the other bilingual areas. So the official languages legislation has not helped the unilingual Canadian, no matter whether he is Francophone or Anglophone, and has made our civil service a type of Janissary civil service based on some sort of ability to speak two languages, or the ability to convince someone that one can do so.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Nonsense.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The official languages legislation can only harden the division of the country into two groups, Francophone and Anglophone. If we are to have two official ' languages in this country we will have to make provision in the civil service in order that a unilingual person, be
(Mr. Ritchie.]
Francophone or Anglophone, can enter the civil service and in his own language proceed through the civil service and go as far as his talents will carry him in his language, without ever having to learn a second language, at least in theory. This will necessitate both French and English language units in the civil service. The number of units in each group will be proportionate to the number of people in each language group in each province.
In no other area has this government created a stronger backlash, particularly in western Canada, than in the area of its official languages policy. It is an intellectual's solution to a very complex problem. There seems to be no way around it except on a numerical basis, setting up within the civil service Anglophone and Francophone language units which are to care for English and French speaking peoples in the two working languages of Canada. The official languages bill has done much to cause disunity in Canada and if the legislation is carried to the fullest extreme it will be a grave factor in bringing about the fragmentation of our Canadian nation.
Mr. Speaker, this government in its four years in office has shown complete indifference toward and lack of understanding of western Canada. Its record in agriculture is dismal. The new tax bill indicates that the government intends to tax the resources of western Canada and its development will be slow until some time in the future. The movement of Air Canada from Winnipeg to Montreal and the concentration of Canadian National Railways in Montreal are designed to further this subservience. The downgrading of the Port of Churchill, a port which would allow the western farmer access to a lever with which to combat the monopoly position of the port of Montreal, has been actively carried on by this government. This is a shortsighted policy because Churchill would not provide much competition to the great port of Montreal. This government's activities in handling our affairs are building for us a sort of nationalistic ghetto. In future we will pay a heavy price, both of an economic and a social nature, for the activities of the government.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Cullen (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, quite candidly, I did not intend participating in this Throne Speech debate because it was my good fortune two years ago to be selected by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to move the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. I know how big an honour that is for a Member of Parliament, particularly for one newly elected as I was in 1968. For that reason, my congratulations to the mover and seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne are heartfelt.
I know the hon. member for Bruce (Mr. Whicher). He comes from Ontario and I know that he spent 12 years in the Ontario Legislature. He established a distinguished record there before seeing fit to move into the federal field. The hon. member had a splendid record in the
February 24, 1972

Ontario legislature. He has brought to this House his dedication and his ideas about the kind of Canada he wants to see.
Where did the hon. member for Bruce, who is Englishspeaking, who does not speak one word of French, who is a veteran, having spent five years overseas, spend part of his holidays? I understand he spent it in Rimouski, Quebec. He went there and tried his best to speak French, because he is convinced that the only way the Englishspeaking Canadian will understand the French-speaking Canadian, and vice versa, is by going into his living room and trying to communicate with him. If he cannot do it in English, he will do it in halting French or in sign language. He will even do it over a bottle of beer. Nevertheless, he will find a way to communicate with his Quebec colleagues. That is where the hon. member for Bruce spent part of his holiday, and I commend him for it.
He did not do it for political advantage; I doubt whether there is one French-speaking Canadian living in the constituency of Bruce. Nevertheless, the hon. member for Bruce went to Quebec and tried to communicate with French Canadians because he is trying to understand what they are saying to those of us who are English Canadians.
They have a lot to teach us, Mr. Speaker. They know how to live, they know about joie de vivre, a term we do not have in the English language. He wanted to learn about them, and when he spoke he must certainly have spoken as a Liberal because that is his political philosophy. Yet he also spoke as a Member of the Parliament of Canada. As I say, he went to Rimouski, I believe, to find out what the people there think about English Canadians and what French Canadians think about English Canada. He did his best to communicate with the people in that province.
My colleague who seconded the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne, the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Lajoie), is a brave man. I think of him, a married man, trying to establish himself in Ontario, largely an English-speaking province. He has eight children, yet he is prepared to offer himself as a Member of Parliament so that he may serve his country. I invite all hon. members to read his speech. His comments are humorous, yet one can see the dedication of this hon. member who has come here seeking to serve his country. That is why I have hope for Canada. In this country there are Englishspeaking Canadians and French-speaking Canadians, and here there is a French-speaking member who came to Ontario. And what did he say about his eight children? They are not French-speaking, they are bilingual. That is the kind of members we have in the House of Commons.
The calibre of the members of the House of Commons is, I think, second to none. It was my good fortune to speak to the former leader of the New Democratic party. I came here as a brand new member. After I had been here for two years I was sitting beside him in the economy section of the aircraft, which is where Members of Parliament travel, and he said our system brought the best, over-all, kind of Members of Parliament to the House of Commons, men who did not come to the House after building up a reputation, but who came here having
Speech from the Throne
everything to look forward to, having established their businesses, be it insurance, farming or the practice of law. He said these were men who could have rested on their laurels, but instead they chose to come here to represent the people.
He said that, member for member, this was the best House of Commons of which he had ever been a member, and he was speaking from the experience of 35 years in provincial and federal governments. So I am proud to be a member of this House and I hope it will be my good fortune to serve in the next Parliament.
I came down with two obligations, as I saw it. No man can be an expert in every field. So, like many members here, I saw fit to serve the veterans and the senior citizens. I think the people who deserve the highest praise are the Hong Kong veterans, because they have broken through one barrier. If a man was a Hong Kong veteran his widow will now get $200 a month pension. Hopefully, we shall raise this in the future. We have heard members on the other side and on this side say that prisoners of war generally speaking should be given something similar, and I am sure they will come before the Veterans Affairs Committee. We had a Veterans Affairs Committee of which I was proud to be a member, and I served briefly as chairman. It did not seek to De a partisan committee, but to serve the Canadian people as a whole.
These are all motherhood things. Let us move on to topics upon which we are not all agreed. Let us get into labour legislation. There has been a concerted and, I think, unfavourable attack on the Labour Code legislation. The situation is that we have decided-and I hope the new legislation will bear this out-that where a technological change of significance is introduced by companies which will have the effect of laying off a significant number of employees, then the collective bargaining agreement will be reopened.
I think this is good legislation. I say so for this reason. Put yourselves in the bargaining room. You have the company representatives on one side of the room and representatives of the workers on the other. The company lads are sitting there, and they know when they are bargaining that they will be introducing a technological change which will have the effect of laying off a significant number of employees, be it 200, 300, 500 or 50, depending on the size of the company. They know, when they are negotiating a pay raise, be it 10, 15 or 20 per cent, that they will not have to pay not only the increase; they will not even have to pay the salaries or the wages of the individuals, of 20 per cent of the people employed by their company. They are not in a position to say, "we are going to give you, in effect, the sleeves of our vests; we are going to give you a 15 per cent pay raise," because they know that in the course of the three years of the agreement 20 per cent of the labour force are not only going to receive the increase but are not going to receive any salary at all.
The fellows representing labour or the union do not know this. So if the company says "Gentlemen, this is something we should tell you; we are going to introduce a technological change which will have the effect of reducing our staff by a significant number," the boys on the other side will say, "We know what the score is and now we can bargain within the terms of reference explained to us."
