February 24, 1972
Speech from the Throne
But if the company fails to do that and says, say a year later, to its employees, "We have brought in a technological change. We do not need 200 of our employees and we shall have to lay them off," then I say it is right in law and it is certainly right in equity that the contract should be reopened so that the employees can go back and say, "Just a minute. We don't think it is right. This is a technological change we did not know anything about, and maybe we should renegotiate the contract we have."
I think this is good legislation. If the company tells the employees or the people bargaining for the employees that it intends to introduce a technological change, the contract will not be reopened. But if it is bargaining knowing that it intends to lay off a certain number of workers, and if it does not tell the people on the other side of the table beforehand, I think we are not playing the game according to the rules and the government has an obligation to step in and make a change. I support this legislation wholeheartedly and I am confident the government will not back away from its present position.
It was my good fortune to serve as Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence. I went into that department wondering how a man who was in the Canadian forces during peacetime maintains his level of competence, and how he has pride, a certain professionalism which he should bring into the job. I was in that job only for about three months but I was convinced that the Canadian forces bring to their job a sense of pride, a sense of professionalism which was the precedent set during wartime by the Royal Canadian Navy, the Royal Canadian Air Force and the Canadian Army.
There is a sense of dedication and professionalism that these men during peacetime still bring to their particular jobs. I think more could be said about this, but unhappily it is not done in peacetime because people seem to think that if you cannot do anything else you can get a job in the Canadian forces. That is not so any more; you have to possess a certain degree of intelligence and education to be a good member of the Canadian armed forces. We happen to be blessed with 80,000 or 90,000 members of the forces who bring with them this degree of dedication. I say, thank God for these men who serve during peacetime, when they do not get the kind of recognition they might during wartime.
I want to speak about another subject, that of the environment. The suggestion has been made that the government is not concerned about pollution and has not taken any action in this field. I supported the idea of appointing a Minister of the Environment. At long last we have a minister whose main obligation is to co-ordinate the areas so that we can do that which is best to control pollution be it of the air, of the land or of our water.
We have good legislation under the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis). We have a situation now where we are trying to clean up the Ottawa River, which means we have to bring the province of Quebec, the province of Ontario and the federal government into reaching some kind of agreement. We are facing a similar situation in the Great Lakes, where we have to deal with two or three provinces, important cities, the government of the United States and various states in the United States. We are endeavouring to do that which is necessary to see that our Great Lakes are cleaned up. Certainly it was a severe
[Mr. Cullen.)
blow to learn that the amount of money to be provided in the United States for pollution control was to be reduced. Reports indicate, however, that this may not have the detrimental effect we thought it might have in so far as pollution control of the Great Lakes is concerned.
There is another area which should receive more publicity, that is, the degree of co-operation between the United States and Canada with respect to the surveillance of the Great Lakes and the fact that some of the ships using the Great Lakes see fit to ignore the fact that if they dump their bilgewater, which has oil in it, or if they dump the other material which has the effect of despoiling the water, it has a tendency to come up on the beaches of the Great Lakes. This is another area in which we need surveillance. If I am driving along and I know a member of the Ontario police force is a mile down the road, I am not going to be speeding. That is what we need in the Great Lakes, a form of sophisticated surveillance.
I am happy that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) has indicated that he is coming to the Sarnia area, to that great area where we have Lake Huron and its beautiful beaches, to see whether we should not think about having some form of aircraft or sophisticated surveillance so that ships either coming down the lakes or going up, or even ships parked in the lakes by reason of some hold-up in the lakes, do not dump their bilgewater or garbage into the Great Lakes and pollute them, with rubbish washing up on the beaches of Lake Huron, be they on the Canadian or on the United States side. But this government is aware of the problems in this area and I am hoping that the kind of surveillance I am looking for'will be provided.
I want to make just one more comment before I conclude. When I ran during the last election campaign I adopted a rather presumptuous campaign slogan which was "Cullen for Canada". It had a nice ring to it and had the alliteration that politicians look for. But for this particular member it had a meaning, too. I ran on the understanding that we were going to have an Official Languages Act, that we would recognize that any Canadian in Canada, be he French or English speaking, could go to any government department and speak his own language. Someone whose mother tongue was French should be able to go to any post office in British Columbia or Ontario and speak French and be understood. By the same token I, as an English-speaking Canadian, should be able to go to the remotest part of Quebec and speak English in a post office or any federal office.
Such a situation does not mean we are ramming French down the throats of English-speaking Canadians. Neither is it ramming English down the throats of French-speaking Canadians. All it means is that a French-speaking, unilingual Canadian is able to go to British Columbia and use his native tongue in any federal office. This is the way it should be if we sincerely believe that this is truly a bilingual country. I support that kind of philosophy completely.
There has been some misrepresentation of the Official Languages Act. Many people have said that it has the effect of spreading French to western Ontario or western Canada, or that it spreads English through Quebec. Nothing could be further from the truth. It is, as I have said,
February 24, 1972

merely ensuring that unilingual Canadians, be they English-speaking or French-speaking, can conduct business in any federal office or government department in their own language.
I for one cannot understand why people are opposed to learning a second language. It was a treat to me. I take French lessons two days a week, which means I have to get up earlier than I normally do. I had a splendid opportunity to learn French when I went to Le College Militaire de Saint Jean. I remember when you, Mr. Speaker, and I celebrated our passing of "legon quatorze". We were both thrilled that at last we could communicate with our French-speaking colleagues. They would come across to our table and ask us for the English word for such-and-such. We were able to communicate with them and have a great time. Last summer I visited Quebec and used my French to get food and lodging. I did not run into any separatism, merely friendship. When they say "hospitalite is spoken here", let me tell you that that is true.
I think Canadians have an obligation to learn the second language, but I would prefer to think that Canadians have the opportunity to speak the second language. You will find no nicer people than the French-speaking Canadians of Quebec, northern Ontario or St. Boniface. Neither will you find any nicer English-speaking Canadians than those in southern Ontario, in the area I represent.

Mr. Speaker, this debate has reflected, particularly in the nature of the amendment that has been moved by my colleague from Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), a disillusionment today that is very worrisome to many of us who have been in Parliament for many years. We have seen the growth of a confrontation of ideology, a confrontation of region, a confrontation of ethnic origin. I use that term very advisedly and with apologies to this House, because I do not believe in a confrontation of ethnic origin.
I as an individual am a product, on my father's side, of generation upon generation of French speakers and Irish
Speech from the Throne
speakers. Much more recently, on my mother's side, my ancestors have come from continental Europe, from Belgium. Like the hon. member for Sarnia (Mr. Cullen), who has just resumed his seat and was also a veteran in the last World War, I married an English girl, as did thousands upon thousands of Canadians. We look upon this sort of linguistic, ethnic confrontation as though it were a plan from the devil to destroy the Canadian nation. There is nothing quite so diabolical as this, to my way of thinking.
I am sure that from Vancouver Island to Newfoundland and from the forty-ninth parallel to the north pole there are hundreds of thousands, indeed millions, of Canadians who think alike. Yet here we are in this day and age exposed to a philosophy, espoused by government, of confrontation; a philosophy of the government that says you are either on this side or on the other side.
